## Source page 2

### Introduction

Swargiya Mahabir Prasad Srivastava was born on Kartik Shukla 2, 1644, according to that, on October 18, 1887, in the village Bijhauli, tehsil Handia, district Allahabad. He passed the High School (1606) and Inter Examinations (1608) from the Kayastha school of Allahabad and the B.S.-C. examination (1610) from Moore College. Due to not being in good financial condition, he took a job. From Kartik month of year 1679, he started writing the 'Vigyanbhashya' of 'Surya-Siddhanta' which was continuously published in the monthly magazine of the Science Council. This ended in year 1667. The Science Council published it in book form in two parts.

He received the Mangalaprasad award and the Chunnulal award for this text.

Upon completion of the first edition of this text, it is being re-published at the request of the readers.

This book, equipped with the 'Vigyan Bhashya Tika', is a priceless treasure of ancient Indian literature and a glorious book of Hindi. 'Surya-Siddhanta' is useful and collectible for all libraries and inquirers.

## Source page 6

### Role

Swami Dayananda gave a comprehensive curriculum of study and teaching to graduates of the Vidya-Layas in 1874 in his immortal text Satyarth Prakash. This course has historical significance because before this arrangement by Rishi Dayananda, there was no comprehensive system of courses in this country. In 1858, three universities were opened in the country—Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay. In 1888, two more universities (after the death of Maharishi Dayananda) were established in Prayag and Lahore. Such examinations of Sanskrit, like that of Kashi, had not begun. Therefore, we can surely say that the entire curriculum method of Rishi Dayananda is the first attempt in this direction. After studying grammar, the Rishi said that he taught Manusmriti, Valmiki Ramayana, Mahabharata, Shad Darshanas, Brahmanas, Upavedas (Ayurveda, Dhanurveda, Gandharvaveda; Arthaveda-Shilpa etc.). Then he wrote that in two years, learn astrology, the theory of the sun, which includes algebra, numbers, geography, astronomy, and geology, as is.

The primary source of astrological subjects is the hymns of the Vedas. The name of Sukta 164 of the first Mandala of Rigveda is Asyavamiya Sukta. The mantra-darshita of this Sukta is Rishi Dirgatamas. This Sukta is the inspirational source of astrology-

Twelve are not the wheel that circulates in the mind of the wise.

O son of fire, do not be deceitful here for seven hundred and twenty-five.

(RV 1/164/11)

The cycle of the sun which has twelve rays, which constantly moves, never tires, does not age, does not die. It has 720 sons (360 days and 360 nights). In the Atharvaveda, they are in the nineteenth section of two Suktas (Suktas 7 and 8), whose sage is Gargya. In this Sukta, the calculation of 27 constellations is given. Taking inspiration from the Vedas, Lagadha Muni composed Vedanga Jyotish, whose verses are found in Rig Jyotish and Yuj-Jyotish. Lagadha's time is considered to be before 600 AD. There is another word for Jyotish for this, Kaal-Vidhan-Shastra (Yuj-Jyotish 3). Lagadha also used the word "Ganit" in this sense, and the glory of this part of Vedanga is expressed as follows—


## Source page 7

### 7

As the splendor of the crest of peacocks and the jewels of snakes are as such, so is the mathematics of the Vedangas.

Yuj: Jyotish, verse 4

The splendor of the crest in the body of the peacock and the glory of the jewel on the head of the snakes are the mathematics of the Vedangas, that is, the mathematics of astrology.

After the Vedangas, many principles of astrology were practiced in the field of Jyotish. Five of these principles are of special importance. Varahamihira discussed them comparatively in his famous work "Panchasiddtantika". The five principles are counted in the following verse—

Polish-Romak-Vasishtha-Sora-Patamahasru Panchasiddhanta:

Latdev analyzed the first two of these. According to Varahamihira, the calculation in the Polish theory is true, and the Romak theory is also almost the same. The true theory of sunlight, i.e., the solar theory or the sun theory, is even clearer than these two. The remaining two, Vasishtha and Patamaha, are false (misled). One edition of Panchasiddtantika was published by Professor Thibaut and Mahamahopadhyaya Sudhakar Dwivedi along with the English translation. The name of Sudhakar ji's Sanskrit commentary is “Panchasiddtantika Prakashika” (Prayag, 15 December 1888).

In the same tradition, Shri Mahavir Prasad Srivastava, an old councilor of the Science Council, Prayag, took up the arduous task of the science commentary of the Sun Theory. This lifetime work of his ended in 1640 AD. The work began in 1622, its first chapter (Madhyamadhikar) was published in 1624. The twelfth chapter was printed in 1631. Work stopped due to lack of funds. The last two chapters were printed in 1640. Thus, this commentary ended in Bhai Tritiya Samvat 1667 B.E. i.e., 1640 AD. This book was published in the science-monthly magazine in small parts, and some copies of the book were also prepared separately. This science commentary of the Sun Theory has been unavailable for the last about 20 years.

The Swadhyay Sansthan has attained this honor, by the immense generosity of the officers of the Science Council, Prayag, which obtained permission for its publication. [A brief excerpt of the introduction written by Sw. Shri Mahavir Prasad Srivastava]

Astrology is the principal part of the Vedas because from it the time of sacrifices is determined. Therefore, in ancient times in Bharata, the study-teaching of astrology was considered meritorious work. It also has another name, Kalavidhyashastra or Kalajnan. According to Kashyap Samhita, there were 18 Acharyas who were the originators of astrology, whose names are:-

1—Surya, 2—Pitamah, 3—Vyasa, 4—Vasishtha, 5—Atri, 6—Parashar, 7—Kashyap, 8—Narad, 9—Garg, 10—Marichi, 11—Manu, 12—Angira, 13—Lomash, 14—Paulish, 15—Chyavan, 16—Yavana, 17—Bhrigu and 18—Shaunak.

The principles and texts of these 18 names are unknown. Many are the doers of both Samhitas and Siddhantas, some only in one subject, and the text of some names is not available in both subjects.

The ancient principles that have been discussed since the time of Varahamihira are 1—Paulish, 2—Romak, 3—Vasishtha, 4—Saur, and 5—Patamah Siddhanta, which Varahamihira has collected in his book named Panch-Siddhantika (approximately 550 AD), in which he also states that the Paulish Siddhanta is clear, the Romak-Siddhanta is close to it, but the Surya-Siddhanta is the clearest, the other two are very corrupted. The direction of these matters has been shown in various places in the Scientific Commentary.

The composition period of Sūrya Siddhānta—there is a great difference of opinion among scholars regarding this. The composition period stated in this book does not make sense by logic because if it had continued in the same way for so ancient a time, twenty-one lakh, sixty thousand years, then why does the question arise that when will the fourteen years of exile of the Pandavas be completed, in the court of Maharaja-adhiraj Duryodhana in the Mahabharata era, where great scholars existed at that time? Even from Bhishma's answer, it is not understandable that he had knowledge of the astrological calculations of a text like Sūrya Siddhānta at that time. However, there is no doubt that the original form of this text is much earlier than Varahamihira, and it is possible that the form seen in Panchasiddhāntika is not the original form, but Varahamihira made some amendments to it. But it is surprising that Aryabhata (476 AD) did not mention it anywhere in his text, from which it is estimated that it was composed around the time of the composition of Aryabhatiya. The form of Sūrya Siddhānta given by Varahamihira is different from the current Sūrya Siddhānta, in which the matters of precession have been added from behind because if the discussion of precession had been in Sūrya Siddhānta before Varahamihira, it must have been included somewhere in Panchasiddhāntika and not been satisfied by writing only that the precession point was in the Nakshatra of Ayana in ancient times, now it is in Punarvasu. Even in the time of Brahmagupta (628-665 AD), the form of Sūrya Siddhānta did not have the matter of precession because in such a situation, Brahmagupta would have certainly discussed it. This point must have been found some time before Bhaskaracārya, but still not in that form as seen now because Bhaskaracārya himself has expressed doubt about its purity. Therefore, it is proven that the original form of the current Sūrya Siddhānta is the same as that given in Panchasiddhāntika and existed even before Varahamihira, or Varaha Sūrya Siddhānta is its modified form and later astrologers have periodically refined it.

Mr. Bentley has done a lot of work in this matter. He calculated the positions of the Sun, Moon, and other planets for different times according to the Sūrya Siddhānta and new observations, and fixed the time of composition of the Sūrya Siddhānta when the portions of the planets according to both calculations become equal. This will be clear from the bracket on page 14 where the inaccuracies of the planets are shown.

From this Bentley derives the result that the Sūrya Siddhānta was written in the late phase of the 11th century. In appearance, it seems very logical and there is no doubt that the author has shown great novelty in it, but in reality, this method is not acceptable without proper examination. I understand sufficiently this point in the words of the publication committee of Burgess's translation:-

The times that Bentley has taken for the relationship of the other planets with the zero error are very close to the times we have calculated, which we have derived by calculating backward from the errors of 1860 AD, and which are given with the commentary of the 67th verse.

Upon comparing these two brackets, it will immediately be seen that Bentley did not derive his decision from the inaccuracies of the absolute positions of the planets, but from the comparison with the position of the Sun. Like other planets, the Sun was not at the position assumed in 3102 B.C., and therefore the motion of the Sun considered in this method is different from the reality because the sidereal year is considered 3 minutes larger. Thus, it can be concluded that the composition of Sūrya Siddhānta took place from 400 AD to 725 AD. Bentley and Burgess also compared the polar stars in Sūrya Siddhānta with the proven polar stars from the modern astronomical measurements to determine the time of Sūrya Siddhānta in this way, but it does not seem so accurate, because the kind of error that the Sūrya Siddhāntakar made regarding the arcs, Brahmagupta and others must have also made. Thus, the upper limit of the period of composition can be extended further. However, the lower limit can be brought up to 1100 AD as proved by Bentley.

The view of Bentley is also supported by the matter of the motion of the ecliptic. In the time of Bhaskara-Charrya, the ecliptic motion written in Sūrya Siddhānta was not as much as in the current Sūrya Siddhānta. It is apparent that the correction of the ecliptic motion was made after Bhaskaraacharya. However, the time of Bhaskaraacharya is 1150 AD.

The author of Sūrya Siddhānta—it has been shown that the polar coordinates of Sūrya Siddhānta do not match the polar coordinates of the Greek astrologers Hipparchus, Talmi, or other Western country astrologers. Therefore, this treatise was not written based on the observations of those people. Its tradition is explained by Vivsvān, that is, by the Sun (see Chapter on Mean Motions verse 8-6), just as the tradition of the Yoga path described in the Bhagavad Gita is explained (see Bhagavad Gita Chapter 4 verse 1-2). Maya is not foreign. He was a resident of India and obtained this knowledge, and the sages also learned from him. This seems to be the secret of the story given in Sūrya Siddhānta. Due to the Brahmashāpa, the story of the Sun God arising in the luminous city is fabricated and is found only in one or two handwritten books.

### ( 23)

is, therefore, it is projected which no one has accepted. If the Sūrya Siddhānta had been obtained by Trideśi, Brahmagupta would surely have written it, because for the Romak Siddhānta, which is undoubtedly foreign, he has written it clearly. There is no trace in the Prakashika ṭīkā of M.M.P. Sudhakar Dwivedi that gives the origin of the Surya-sūrvāda, so it cannot be said who wrote it and on what basis. The writing in Nityānanda1 that it was written when the 3600 years of Kali Yuga had passed, i.e., in the year 421 or 466 AD, when Aryabhata wrote his Aryabhatiya, is a delusion. Perhaps because of this delusion, Muniśvara also considered Aryabhata the author of the Sūrya Siddhānta. Alberuni's statement that it is a delusion that Latāchārya or Laṭsiṃha made it2 is because neither Varāhamihira nor Brahmagupta considered Latāchārya the author of the Sūrya Siddhānta. According to Varāhamihira, Latāchārya is an interpreter of the Romak and Polish theories. Latā's measurements3 are from the sunset time of Yavanpura. Thus, it is apparent that all the estimations regarding the time of composition and author of the Sūrya Siddhānta are not proven. Based on internal evidence, it can only be said that its growth started around 400 AD and ended by 1200 AD. Initially, Varāhamihira must have expanded (amended) it. Then other modifiers tried to make it Up-to-date by taking advantage of the observations of Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Manjula, etc. This amendment continued until Rangnath ji wrote its commentary and bound its verses. Some more verses are found in Madhav Purohit's commentary, don't know if they were written on the basis of an old text or just added.

Scientific Commentary—some people interpret the second verse of the ninth verse to mean that the scripture that the Sun God taught to the sages is that same scripture without any change, only a difference in the time of saying. But if this were the meaning, what was the need to say that there is a difference in time? What was said in the first verse was sufficient. Therefore, the more reasonable meaning of this verse is that if there is any difference in the Jyotiḥ-shastra previously stated and the one being stated at this time, it is due to time, and there is no essential difference. How can there be a difference due to time? The reason is that the Jyotiḥ-shastra is an experimental science and some subtle errors remain in the experiment, which is called experimental error. This error accumulates in Jyotiḥ-shastra year by year and after hundreds of years it takes a very large form; therefore, it has to be revised from time to time, which is called seed-transformation. From this perspective, this sentence was said by Suryāṁśa Puruṣa, for which there are 21 verses named 'Bijopanayana' in the last chapter of the Surya Siddhānta, which Rangnath Ji and Pan. Indranarayan Dwivedi Ji have not considered as a commentary and have explained the reason for not considering it as a commentary, which is that how the seed-transformations are done by the Sun God in the scripture spoken by the Sun God. But Rangnath Ji, while explaining the 6th verse in his gūḍhārtha-prakāśikā commentary, also state that some difference occurs upon taking time. His sentences are as follows:

And also by the movements of time, if there are some celestial bodies, then in the time between the ages, the scriptures were revealed by the compassionate ones for the purpose of the planetary movements, as in the subsequent scriptures, the meaning of which is. Scientific Commentary—When a healthy person is sitting comfortably, the time it takes to inhale and exhale air (life air) naturally is called Pran. This is the smallest unit that could be measured at that time. There was no means to measure less time than this at that time; therefore, it was called abstract. Now such clocks are made by which the measurement of that unit is easy, which are called abstract. In one lunar day, 60 clocks = 60 X 60 shadows = 60 X 60 X 60 Pran or 21600 Pran exist. Similarly, in 1 day, 24 hours = 24 X 60 minutes = 24 X 60 X 60 seconds or 86400 seconds exist. Therefore, there are 4 seconds in 1 Pran. Everyone knows how easy it is to measure a second when the hand of the clock is attached to it. There are also such clocks by which the fifth or tenth part of 1 second can be easily known. However, the tenth part of 1 second is the same as the fortieth part of 1 Pran. Therefore, some units below Pran can also be called concrete nowadays.

Pran is also called Asu. In the Siddhānta-Shiromani of the famous astrologer Bhaskaraacharya ji, the second definition of Pran is given in the words of Chandas-shastra—the time taken to pronounce one Guru letter is called Pran ten times that time. A Guru letter is that which has a conjunct letter after it, such as Sanuswar, Visargant, Dirgha, and the short letter.

There is also a name for a unit of weighing, which is like four tole.

This word reveals that the 12 months that make up a year are the solar months. The year of Chandra, Nakshatra, or Sawan months is not.

Nakshatra Ahuratra—Nakshatra means star, star-group and the 27th part of the cycle on which the sun appears to revolve once in a year. Note down the time of rising of any star by looking at the clock and see when that star rises again. If the clock is correct, the time between these two risings is approximately 23 hours 56 minutes and 4 seconds. This is called Nakshatra Ahuratra or only Nakshatra day. This is always the same, it does not increase or decrease, if the very subtle motion of the stars is not considered. Therefore, astrologers calculate time from this.

## Source page 31

The value is not the same. Therefore, the value of the mean Sāvan day is the time known by clocks.

The Indav Tithi or Chandra Tithi—the time when the moon reaches very close to the sun while revolving in the sky is the new moon. The time between one new moon and the next new moon is called the lunar month. Its mean value is 26.530587646 of the mean Sāvan day. After the new moon, the moon moves further towards the east from the sun, and when it moves 12 degrees further, the first tithi (pariva) passes. When the difference is between 12 and 24 degrees, it remains duija. When the moon is ahead of the sun from 24 to 36 degrees, it remains tīja. When the difference is between 178 and 180 degrees, it is the full moon. When the moon is ahead from 180 to 162 degrees, it is the 16th tithi or pariva (pratipada). Duija remains from 1620 to 2040, etc. After the full moon, the moon moves back by 2 hours (48 minutes) each day from sunset. The 14, 15 days from the full moon to the new moon are called the dark fortnight. The new moon is also called the 30th tithi, which is why 30 is written for the new moon in Panchangs.

Sārmāsa—the path along which the sun travels while revolving in the sky is called the ecliptic. Its twelfth part is called the Rāshi. The center of the solar system, at the time it enters one Rāshi and moves to another Rāshi, that time is the transit of the second Rāshi. The time between one transit and the next transit is called Sārmāsa. The 12 solar months are different in magnitude; the reason for this is that the motion of the sun is not always the same. When the motion of the sun is fast, it completes one Rāshi quickly and the solar month is shorter. Conversely, when the motion of the sun is slow, the solar month is larger.

The number of types of months is equal to the number of types of years; a lunar year of twelve lunar months, a Sawan year of twelve Sawan months, and a solar year of twelve solar months. Our astrologer tradition has believed this. However, the direct meaning of the second part of the 13th verse is that there is a year of 12 months, which is called the divine day. Therefore, the year of twelve months mentioned is not other months, only solar months. This proves that the Surya Siddhanta discusses only the solar year and considers the solar year as the year, not others.

It is stated that the North Pole of the Earth is the abode of the gods and the South Pole is the abode of demons. Therefore, the North Pole is called Deva-loka and the South Pole is called Asur-loka. At the time when the sun comes to the equator, day and night are equal. This phenomenon occurs only twice a year. The sun remains north of the equator for 6 months and south for 6 months. In the first half, the day is longer and the night is shorter in the northern hemisphere and the day is shorter and the night is longer in the southern hemisphere. In the second half, it is exactly the opposite. However, when the sun remains north of the equator, it is visible on the North Pole (on Mount Sumeru) for 6 months and not visible at the South Pole at this time. Therefore, this half is called the day of the gods and the night of the demons. When the sun remains south of the equator for 6 months, the gods are not seen at the North Pole and the demons are seen equally at the South Pole for 6 months. Therefore, this half is called the night of the gods and the day of the demons. Therefore, our 12 months are like one yuga of the gods or demons.

Scientific Commentary—the 14th verse states that there is a divine year of 360 days for gods or asuras. The 13th verse states that one day of the gods is like one solar year, so it is clear that one year of the gods is equal to 360 solar years. According to the 15th verse, a Chaturyuga is a period of 12000 divine years or 12000 X 360 (i.e., 432000) solar years. Chaturyuga is also called Mahayuga. In one Mahayuga there are four Yugas: Satya Yuga; Treta, Dvapara, and Kali Yuga, which is why it is also called Chaturyuga. In Satya Yuga, Dharma has four stages, in Treta three stages, in Dvapara two stages, and in Kali Yuga one stage. Similarly, in one Mahayuga, Satya Yuga has four parts, Treta has three parts, Dvapara has two parts, and Kali Yuga has one part. Therefore,

Divine years in solar years, Satya Yuga, Treta, 4800 1728000, Dvapara, 3600 1296000, Kali Yuga, 2400 864000, Mahayuga 1200 432000

Both sandhyas of Satya Yuga are equal to the sixth part, so one sandhya (period) is equal to the twelfth part. The sandhya at the beginning of the Yuga and the sandhya at the end are called Adi Sandhya and Ant Sandhya. Their values are as follows:-

In divine years in solar years, the beginning and end sandhyas of Satya Yuga are 400 144000, of Treta 300 108000, of Dvapara 200 72000, of Kali Yuga 100 360000

Just as there are two sandhyas in the morning and evening in one Ahoraatra, there are two sandhyas in each Yuga, one at the beginning and one at the end.

Translation—(25) The planets, moving with the swift constellations, always fall behind in their respective orbits by the same amount while moving towards the west; (26) Therefore, they appear to move towards the east and their daily motion also appears different according to the circumference of the orbits; Therefore, the lunar cycle also completes in this different time, that is, (27) in a short time of swift movement and in a long time of slow movement. The cycle that is completed at the end of Revati is called bhagaṇa.॥25-27॥

Scientific Commentary—the principle of the motion of the planets is explained in these three shlokas; therefore, these are of great importance. From these, it is revealed in brief what the ancient Indian astronomers thought about the planets. It is stated in the 25th shloka that all the stars seen in the sky are moving towards the west with the planets; but due to the very fast movement of the constellations, the planets lag behind and appear to move in the easterly direction. The speed of their movement towards the east is the same, but because the extent of their orbits is different, their motion also appears different. The secret of this will be revealed in the following figure—suppose that the inner circle in the given figure is 10 inches and the outer is 15 inches, and suppose that two ants moving at a speed of 1 inch per second orbit the inner and outer circles from the positions of x and y, which are in a straight line with the center; then it is clear that the ant moving on the outer circle will complete one orbit in 15 seconds and the ant moving on the inner circle will complete one orbit in 10 seconds. This proves that when moving with the same linear motion, the revolution of orbits of different sizes will take different times. But in the 27th shloka


## Source page 39

It has been said that fast-moving planets complete their orbits in a short time and slow-moving planets in a long time. There seems to be some opposition here, but this is not an opposition; because the motion stated in the first verse is the planimetric motion and the motion in this verse is the angular (Angular velocity). One revolution is of 360 degrees; therefore, one inch of the outer circle makes an angle of 360/15 = 24^° at the center and one inch of the inner circle makes an angle of 360/10 = 36^°. Therefore, although the rectilinear motion of ants is the same at 1 inch per second, although their angular motion is different per second. The outer ant moves at 24^° per second and the inner at 36^°. Therefore, it is clear that the fast-moving ones will complete their orbits in less time and the slow-moving ones in more time.

In the 27th verse, the definition of revolution is also given. When the planet moves towards the east, starting from the end of the constellation Revati, and after completing one revolution, it comes back to the end of Revati, then it completes one revolution (constellation group which is 27). Therefore, revolution is also called a circuit.

According to this principle, it must be assumed that there is a special relationship between the distances of the planets and their periods of revolution. The farther a planet is, the longer its period of revolution (time taken to complete a revolution) is. This relationship is stated very briefly here. Its full explanation will be given in the twelfth chapter called Bhūgolāyādhya, comparing the principles of Indian and Western astrologers.

When the linear motions of all the planets are assumed to be equal, it can be easily proven what is the mutual relationship between the distances of the planets; because it is not difficult to know how many days each planet takes to complete one revolution. When it is known that Saturn takes a revolution in a coarse manner in 30 years and the Sun in 1 year and their linear motions are equal, then it is self-evident that the orbit of the Sun is 30 times the orbit of Saturn; because in 30 years the Sun travels 30 times its orbit and Saturn is able to complete its orbit only once. Therefore, the orbit of Saturn = 30 X orbit of the Sun. That is, the distance of Saturn from the Earth is 30 times the distance of the Sun. Similarly, the distances of the other planets can also be known.

It has been known from the current observations that the relationship between the mutual distances of the planets is not so simple, nor are their linear motions the same. Now it is proven that the distance of Saturn from the Earth is almost 10 times the distance of the Sun from the Earth.

Scientific Commentary—these are the units for measuring angles. The entire zodiac cycle is called revolution. If twelve equal parts are made of this revolution, each part is called rashi. The thirtieth part of rashi is an degrees, the sixty-th part of degrees is arcminutes, and the sixty-th part of arcminutes is arcseconds. Revolution and rashi are used only for that celestial cycle in which the sun appears to revolve around the earth in its plane and other planets revolve somewhat shifted. However, degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds are also used in measuring other angles. Nowadays, the way to write degrees in short is that a small circle slightly to the right of the digit indicating the magnitude of degrees.


## Source page 41

They write, for writing the arts, they draw a crooked line slightly to the right of the number and a similar two slanted lines for the obliquity; for example, if one wants to write 5 degrees 16 minutes and 50 seconds, they write 5°16'50".

There is a proportional relationship in the units of measuring angles and time. The time it takes the Sun to complete one revolution is one year, the time it takes for one zodiac sign to move is one month, the time it takes for one degrees to move is one day, the time it takes for one arcminutes to move is approximately one hour, and the time it takes for one arcseconds to move is approximately the same as a moment.

Scientific Commentary—It would be good to state here what is the old tradition for writing numbers among us. Some words have been fixed to write the numbers one, two, three, four, etc., in verse. Those or their synonyms are placed in order according to the rule 'ankānām vāmato gatiḥ', that is, the word indicating the number written in the unit place is written first, then the word indicating the tens place.


## Source page 42

The word indicating the number being referred to, and the word indicating the place in the hundreds, are kept in sequence. For example, if 325 is said, the word indicating 5 is written first, such as Panch, Ishu, Margana, etc., and after it, the word indicating 2 is written, such as Dvi, Ashvi, Yama, etc., then the word indicating 3 is written, such as Tri, Agni, Shikhi, etc. In this way, 325 can be written as Panchaavashikhi or Ishuyamagni. This is the same procedure for writing numbers in Sūrya Siddhānta, Brahmasphuta-Siddhānta, and Siddhanta-Shiromani. The ways of writing numbers in the Aryabhatiya of the first Aryabhata and the Mahā-Siddhānta of the second Aryabhata are different from this.

The number of revolutions of the planets in one great age are given above according to the Sūrya Siddhānta. According to the theories of Aryabhata and Brahmagupta, there are some differences in the values of the great age revolutions, and the values of the revolutions that are known with the help of sūkṣmayaṃtroṃ nowadays do not match any theory but have only a slight variation. On the next page, we give a comparative view of the values of the Sūrya Siddhānta, the Brahmagupta-Siddhānta, and the modern revolutions, from which it will be apparent how little the difference is between the revolution periods calculated by our ancient astrologers and the revolution periods calculated by the modern sūkṣmayaṃtroṃ. The time taken for a planet to complete one revolution or orbit is called the revolution period. The method for calculating this is as follows according to the theory: divide the number of revolutions of that planet in one great age by the solar years of the great age, then 1 revolution period (in solar years) will be obtained. Now, you can write this either in decimal fractions or in Sawan days. The easiest way to calculate the revolution period in Sawan days is to divide the number of Sawan days in the great age by the great age revolution, the remainder is the number of Sawan days. Make the rest into hours, minutes, etc. Just as there are 60 minutes in 1 hour, so it can be imagined that there are 60 vipala in 1 pala and 60 prativipala in 1 vipala.

## Source page 46

In the sky, a place does not remain fixed but keeps moving towards the east with a slow motion. The Moon completes one orbit in approximately 3232 Sawan days. The higher or apogee of other planets also move towards the east with even slower speeds. This imagination is not used nowadays. It has been proven by mathematics that the Moon and the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, and the path of revolution is not circular but elliptical. Before saying anything about this, it is necessary to state some properties of the ellipse. The ellipse is a figure (Figure 3). The upper axis is called the major axis and the lower axis is called the minor axis, and the point where these two axes meet is called the center of the ellipse. At the center, the minor axis and the major axis have two equal parts. There are two such points on the major axis at equal distances from the center, which if connected to any point P, A, or B of the ellipse, then P + A = B + BA = PN + PI. These two points are called the focus of the ellipse. If the Moon's orbit is assumed, then the position of the Earth will not be there. From point N, the distance of the Moon's orbit is maximum at point U and minimum at point B, so point U will be the higher or apogee of the Moon and point B will be the lower of the Moon. If the position of the apogee is known, the position of the lower can be easily known, as it always remains at 180° from the higher.

Similarly, the Earth, Mars, Mercury, Venus, etc., also revolve in an ellipse around the Sun, and the Sun remains at the focus of these orbits. Why the motion is very slow at a high place and very fast at a low place is due to the variation in the force of attraction. When the planet is at a high place, the force of attraction is very small due to the very large distance, which slows down the planet's motion, and when it is at a low place, the force of attraction is very large due to the very small distance, which makes the planet's motion very fast. Many rules have been known regarding this, which are famous by the name of Kepler's laws; these will be discussed in due place in the second chapter named Chapter on True Positions.

Node—the path on which the Sun moves and revolves the sky in 1 year is called the circle of declination. Similarly, the path on which the Moon moves and orbits the Earth is called the lunar orbit. The circle of declination and the lunar orbit are not in the same plane and are not parallel; therefore, these two orbits appear to meet at two points; just as the strings of two flying kites meet at one point even though they remain very far from each other.

When it reaches its node, it either moves towards the north or/or the south of the ecliptic. The node to which it moves towards the north is called the Ascending node and the node to which it moves towards the south is called the Descending node. The Ascending node is also called Rahu and the Descending node is also called Ketu. When the Moon is near these nodes at the time of the full moon or new moon, a lunar eclipse or solar eclipse occurs; that is why it is imagined that Rahu and Ketu are demons caused by the eclipse. Some people consider the tip of the Earth's shadow as Rahu and the tip of the Moon's shadow as Ketu; but this is an illusion.

The positions of these nodes are also not fixed but seem to shift towards the west. This method is given to know the period of the Sun's revolution—

Draw a circle on a plane and mark the directions in it. When the Sun is in the Uttarayana position, on the day when it rises a little south of the east, find the Sun by passing through the nail embedded in the center of the circle. After this, one should calculate the rising of the Sun for one year. The Sun will rise 365 times in a year. The last rising will be a little south of the rising place of the first day. Write the difference between these two. Find the Sun by rising on the second day. On this day, it will rise a little north of the east. Also know how much north it rises from the rising place of the previous day. Then, by the ratio, find out that when such a much north moves in 60 hours, then how much time has passed for the first difference. In this way, 15 hours 30 minutes 22 minutes 30 seconds and 365 Sawan days, the Sun rises in the same place as it did at the beginning of the year. Therefore, this time is the period of the Sun's revolution. Then, by the ratio, find out that when there are such Sawan days in 1 year, then how many Sawan days are there in 1 Kalpa years, etc.

On the third day, that star will rise 2 times the time difference from the sun, that is 3 minutes 56 seconds earlier, i.e., 7 minutes 52 seconds before. On the fourth day, it will rise three times earlier than that, and on the 16th day, it will rise fifteen times earlier, i.e., 56 minutes and 1 minute less 1 hour earlier. In this way, after lagging behind, on the 361st day, i.e., after 360 sidereal days, that star will rise 24 minutes less, 24 hours earlier, and after 366 sidereal days, the whole 24 hours, i.e., 1 day earlier, when the sun and that star will be together again. Therefore, in the time it takes the constellation to complete 366 revolutions, the sun rises 1 time less and completes one revolution in that time. Therefore, the sun rises 366-1 times in one revolution period (in 1 solar year). Similarly, one should understand about the rises of other planets.

Scientific Commentary—The name of the day is given on the name of the planet which is considered the lord of the first hour (hora) at the beginning of the day. For example, the lord of the first hour of Sunday is Ravi, the lord of that day is Ravi, the lord of the month that starts with Sunday is Ravi, and the lord of the year that starts with Sunday is also Ravi.

To know which planet is the lord of which hour(hour), one should understand the sequence in which the lords of the hours change. Saturn is farther from the Earth than all the planets, then Jupiter is nearest to it, Mars is nearest to Jupiter, Sun is nearest to Mars, Venus is nearest to Sun, Mercury1 is nearest to Venus, and the Moon is nearest to Mercury. The lords of the hours change in this sequence. If the lord of the first hour is Saturn, then the lord of the second hour is Jupiter, the third is Mars, the fourth is the Sun, the fifth is Venus, the sixth is Mercury, the seventh is the Moon, the eighth is Saturn, and so on in sequence. However, the name of the day should be Saturday on the day when the lord of the first hour is Saturn. Therefore, the lord of the second hour of Saturday is Jupiter, the lord of the third hour is Mars, etc. In this way, the same sequence of lords restarts after every seven hours. Therefore, the lord of the 22nd hour of Saturday is Saturn, the 23rd is Jupiter, the 24th is Mars, and the lord of the hour after the 24th should be the Sun. But this 25th hour is the first hour of the next day whose lord is the Sun, so after Saturday comes Sunday. The lord of the second hour of Sunday is Venus, the third is Mercury, the fourth is the Moon, and so on in sequence, the lord of the 11th and 18th 25th hours is also the Moon. But the 25th hour is the first hour of the next day, so the next day falls under the name of the lord of this hour, which is Wednesday. In this way, the naming of other days has also been done2.

The reason why after Saturday comes Sunday and after Sunday comes Monday and after Monday comes Tuesday is now clear. In the order of the planets, Saturn is the fourth planet from the Sun, the Moon is the fourth planet from the Sun, Mars is the fourth planet from the Moon. Fourth method: Knowing the longitude by sending news by electricity—If there is such a relation between two places that news can be sent from one place to another by electricity, then the longitude of these two places can be easily known because the time taken for the electrical news to reach is so short that any inaccuracy that may occur is not like an error.

Suppose one wants to know the longitude of Lucknow from Kashi. The observers of both cities should keep the same type of clock, as if the clock of one tells the time of Sawan, then the clock of the other also tells the time of Sawan. Both clocks should be reconciled with their local time so that each clock can accurately tell the local time of its place. Since Kashi is to the east of Lucknow, the local time of Kashi will be ahead of the local time of Lucknow, and the difference between these two is the longitude of Kashi from Lucknow. At the time when the clock of Kashi shows 'S1' time, a signal should be sent from Kashi. At the time when this signal reaches Lucknow, the time on the clock of Lucknow should be seen. If the time in this clock is 'S2' and it is assumed that the signal reached Lucknow at the same moment it was sent from Kashi, then the longitude of Kashi from Lucknow will be proved by the equation written below:-

```text
d1 = s1 - s2
```

But the value of the difference in longitude that will be obtained from this equation will be some less than the actual longitude because some time must necessarily pass for the electrical signal to reach from Kashi to Lucknow. If the value of this time is 'y' and the actual longitude from Kashi to Lucknow is 'd', then the form of the aforementioned equation will be:-

d = (s1 + y) - s2 = d1 + y (7)

It is natural to imagine that when the planet is 180^° less than the apogee and remains towards the west, the apogee pulls it towards the mean position. Therefore, by performing a negative calculation in the mean position, the true position of the planet is obtained. As the planet moves further away from the apogee, the true motion increases accordingly; therefore, it was understood that the attraction of the apogee increases and decreases according to proximity.

After this, Newton proved that universal gravitation is the cause of all this. The three laws on which Newton proved this are called the laws of motion, are famous by that name, and are:-

First Law—If no external force is applied, every object either remains in its state of rest or moves in a straight line with uniform motion.

Second Law—The change in motion is according to the force applied and this change occurs in the direction of the force applied.

Third Law—To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction, meaning that for every action, there is a reaction in the opposite direction, i.e., the same action but in the opposite direction.

These laws are self-evident. For more information, one should read any book of Dynamics.

Translation—(6) The planets like the Moon etc. displace north or south by their velocity due to the deviation from their node or Rahu ecliptic. (7) When the node is less than 6 degrees or 180° from the planet, it removes the north from the ecliptic, and when it is less than 6 degrees from the planet to the east, it removes the south from the ecliptic.

Sūrya Siddhānta—the simple meaning of these two shlokas is that by looking at the positions of the planet and its node, one should understand whether the planet is exactly on the ecliptic or is shifted some north or south from it. If both the planet and the node are at the 'same place', it should be understood that the planet is on the ecliptic. If the planet is ahead of the node, i.e., east, but not more than 180^° away, then it will be shifted north from the ecliptic, and if the planet is behind the node, i.e., west, but not more than 180^° away, then it will be shifted south from the ecliptic. The reason for this is not the attraction or repulsion of Rahu, but rather that the orbit of a planet is not in the plane of the ecliptic, so the planet does not always remain on the ecliptic. The two points where the planet's orbit and the ecliptic seem to meet are called the node. When the planet is at these two points of its orbit, then it appears on the ecliptic, otherwise the ecliptic

Translation—(14) I respectfully state that the rules by which the planets attain the apparent equality in these motions, that is, they appear directly in the place of the node, are the rules by which they come to be seen, and I say these rules are known by mathematics.

Sūrya Siddhānta - this verse is of great importance. It proves that our ancient Acharyas used to determine the true positions of the planets so that there would be no difference in mathematics and direct observation. For this, subtle rules were made in the Chapter on True Positions. However, as I have explained in the Scientific Commentary of the 6th verse of the Chapter on Mean Motions, whether the instruments are gross or subtle, some experimental error remains in determining them, so a difference occurs in time, which requires periodic revision. This is called 'seed' correction. For example, suppose a clock slows down by one second per day, then in 60 days it will be 1 minute and in 1 year it will be 6 minutes behind. But in practice, it will be said that the clock is very pure; because the difference of 1 minute in 60 days or 1 second per day is not like (the difference). If this difference always occurred and the clock was not revised, then in many years such a difference would occur that it would be impossible to consider it as not like (the difference), and revision would have to be done. Just as a difference of 1 second per day in a clock can take a very large form in some time, similarly, in the periods of revolution of the Sun, Moon, etc., the difference of even 1 moment becomes very large in hundreds of years. This is why the seed correction has to be done. The practice of making revisions in between was accepted by our ancient Acharyas, whose incarnations I will give below; but there has been a difference of opinion on this subject for some days. One side says that there is no right to make any commentary or revision on the ancient texts; whatever is in them should be accepted as is. The other side says that revision is entirely appropriate. The arguments of both sides, as I have found them, are given below:-

The difference between two points of a circle can be shown in two ways. If the difference between the points m, ma, mi, and mi is not measured in the direction of the arrow in figure 15, then it will be um; uma, umi, and umi in sequence. But if the difference between these points is measured in the opposite direction from u, then the difference between u and m is 360°—um, the difference between ma and m is 360°—uma, the difference between mi and m is 360°—umi and the difference between mi and m is 360°—umi. The direction indicated by the arrow in the figure is called the opposite or apasvya direction in Sanskrit texts, nowadays it is called 'positive' or 'direction opposite to the clock'. People living to the north of the celestial equator see the sun, moon, and planets, etc., moving in this direction in their orbits. The opposite direction is called vilom, pratilom, savya, and nowadays 'negative' or 'clock direction' in Sanskrit. Due to the daily motion of the Earth, people living in the northern hemisphere see the sun, moon, stars, etc., moving in this direction. In Sūrya Siddhānta, the method of knowing the difference between the planets from the epicycle apogee or apogee, which are in sequence the fast kendra or slow kendra, is stated to be measured in the opposite or negative direction. Therefore, it is said that the mean planet should be subtracted from the epicycle apogee or apogee. However, many other scholars like Brahmagupta, Bhaskaraacharya have written to measure the difference between the mean planet and the apogee from the opposite direction and the difference between the epicycle apogee and the mean planet from the opposite direction. The reason for this is that the mean planet moves in the opposite direction because it is more rapidly moving from the apogee, and the epicycle apogee moves in the opposite direction because it is more rapidly moving from the mean planet; therefore, the mean planet moves in the opposite direction from the epicycle apogee. Whether the difference between the mean center or the fast kendra is measured, both have the same meaning. Bhaskaraacharya's method is natural and some of the Sūrya Siddhānta are misleading.

Subtract the mandocca from this first correction yukta madhyama planet, consider the remainder as the maṃda kendra, and make the maṃda phala. Half of this maṃda phala, whatever results from adding or subtracting to the first correction yukta madhyama planet, is the second correction yukta madhyama planet. Subtract again from the mandocca and consider the remainder as the dūsarā maṃda kendra, and make the dūsarā maṃda phala. Whatever results from adding or subtracting to the madhyama planet is called the maṃda true planet. Subtract the śīghraphala from the śīghrocca to find the fast kendra and śīghraphala, and whatever results from adding or subtracting this śīghraphala to the maṃda true planet is called the true planet.

The rule for knowing the true planets in Sūrya Siddhānta is this. Other commentators have acted in some different ways, for which there is no need to compare. (46) Multiply the sun's meridian (mean position) by the daily true motion of the planet and divide the product by 12 quantities of arc, that is, 21600 arcs, and add or subtract this from the planet's true position (if the sun's mean position is positive) or subtract (if the sun's mean position is negative), so the planet will be visible in the true midnight.

Scientific Commentary—at the time when the mean sun comes on the meridian circle, that time is the mean noon and at the time when the true sun comes on the meridian circle, that time is the true noon. Similarly, at the time when the mean sun is in the nether (the part of the meridian circle that is below the horizon) there is the mean midnight and at the time when the true sun is in the nether there is the true midnight. From this it is apparent that the true midnight will be as much earlier or later as the true noon will be in the nether as the true sun will be in the nether as the mean sun. But the difference between the true and mean sun is called the mean motion; therefore, in the time it takes for a segment of the meridian circle similar to the mean motion to cross the meridian, the true midnight will be as much earlier or later.

As much as the planet will move in this time, by adding or subtracting the mean midnight time in the true midnight time, the true midnight time will be the true midnight time. To make a subtle calculation, it should first be known how long the arc of the ecliptic or the violation of the meridian will take for the mean motion, but even not doing so results in very little inaccuracy. Therefore, in short, all that is to be done is that in the time it takes to violate the meridian of the geocentric cycle, the planet moves forward at the same speed as its daily motion, so in the time it takes to violate the ecliptic of the mean motion, what will be the speed of the planet.

Translation—(47) By subtracting the daily motion of the apogee of the moon from its mean daily motion, and taking the action told in (48 46 shlokas), the apparent daily motion of the moon is obtained by subtracting or adding from the mean daily motion. Just as by giving the correction of the mean fruit in the mean planet, the mean true planet is obtained, similarly by giving the correction of the motion of the mean or the motion of the mean fruit in the mean daily motion, the mean true motion is found. According to Kepler's law, to know the true position of a planet, it first has to be seen where the planet, which is elliptical in shape in its orbit and whose focus is the Sun itself, is. Then it has to be known where that planet will appear from the Earth at that time.

Suppose the orbit of a planet is elliptical and R is the position of the attractive Sun, which is at the focus of the ellipse. The beginning of the revolution of the planet is considered from the time when the planet is at the nearest distance from the Sun, i.e., at A, and if the planet appears at point G at a distance of 'D' from that time, then A-G is called the apogee of the planet, which will be denoted by the letter S hereafter.

It is stated there that one nakṣatra-ahorātra is equal to 21600 of asu or pranas, and the sāvana day is usually 4 minutes or 10 pals or 56 pranas more than the nakṣatra-ahorātra because the sun moves approximately 1 degree towards the east per day while the constellations or stars remain in the same place. Just as the time between one sunrise and the next sunrise is called sāvana day, similarly, the time from the time a planet rises in the east to the time it rises again on the next day is called that planet's ahorātra. If the planet is in the direct motion, its ahorātra will be more than the nakṣatra-ahorātra, and if it is retrograde, it will be less. The method of knowing how much more or less the planet's ahorātra is than the nakṣatra-ahorātra is explained in this verse. According to how much the planet moves forward or backward during the day, the planet's ahorātra will be more or less than the nakṣatra-ahorātra. In the third chapter named Chapter on the Three Problems, in verses 41-43, this is elaborated.

In this chapter, many methods of obtaining information about direction, country (place), and time from the sun's zenith are described. Only one instrument is used for the zenith, which is called gnomon. A straight pointed rod of a hard metal or ivory was placed vertically on level ground, and all work was done from its shadow. This is called the gnomon. The Yantradhyaya describes other instruments, but in this place, only the gnomon is discussed. It is clear that the image of the sun appears very large, and the tip of the shadow of the gnomon cannot be determined with much subtlety, so the things that can be known from the gnomon are some gross ones. Nowadays, more subtlety can be achieved by sighting with a telescope, but in ancient times, the gnomon was very useful. Our astrologers have shown great skill in obtaining the subtlety that could be achieved by sighting with it. There is no doubt in this at all.

Some such things have also been invented with the help of the gnomon instrument, without which knowledge of direction, country, and time remains coarse, so there is a need to discuss them as well. Scientific Commentary—The common point on the ecliptic where the sun comes from the north of the ecliptic and the tropics is called the vernal equinox. When the sun reaches 60 degrees beyond the vernal equinox, its northward movement stops and it begins to return towards the south. At this time, the onset of the southward motion begins. Therefore, the point where the sun turns to the south is called the summer solstice. The time when the sun continues to move towards the south from the beginning of the southward motion, which is similar to 6 months, is called the southward motion. After 3 months from the beginning of the southward motion, the sun comes again on the vernal equinox. This point is called the autumnal equinox because the autumn season begins at this time. The sun continues to move towards the south for 600 further, then turns back to the north. The point where the sun begins to return to the north is called the winter solstice. The onset of the northward motion begins from this time. The southward and northward points are called the apogees. In Figure 36, the order of V, D, SH, and U are vernal equinox, southward motion point, autumnal equinox, and winter solstice. The circle that occurs on the apogees, celestial poles, and latitudes is called the solstitial colure. In Figure 36, the circle of V, D, SH, U is the solstitial colure.

The knowledge of the movement of the vernal equinox was known to the Greek astronomer Hipparchus seventy years before the Vikram era. While making a list of the stars, he found that the difference between each star in this list and the list made one and a half hundred years earlier was an additional 2 degrees. From this, he concluded that the vernal equinox is receding. The annual motion of the vernal equinox that he calculated was less than 3 less than 36 degrees. Ptolemy determined this motion of the vernal equinox in the beginning of the third century of Vikram. After this, there was no further advancement in Greek astrology regarding the movement of the vernal equinox and other matters.

But a prince named Albatauni of Arabia, who was a skilled astronomer, determined the annual motion of the vernal equinox with some accuracy of about 637 AD. Shankar Balakrishna Dikshit writes that Albatauni had determined the annual motion of the equinox to be 55.5 degrees. After this, Nasiruddin established a observatory near the northern western border of present-day Iran and determined the annual motion of the vernal equinox to be 51 degrees at the beginning of the 14th century Vikram.

However, this is not the case. Because the Earth is rotating on its axis at a very high speed, the angle between the planes of the equator and the ecliptic will always remain approximately the same, and the pole and the south will continue to revolve in a circle around each other.

### The First Method of Knowing the Equinoctial Shadow

> एवं विषुवति छाया स्वदेशे या दिनार्धजा ।
> दक्षिणोत्तरयोरेव सा तत्र विषुवत्प्रभा ॥१२॥

Translation—(12) In this way, on the day the Sun is on the equinoctial circle, the shadow cast by the gnomon on the north-south line of a place at noon is the equinoctial influence or equinoctial shadow of that place.

Scientific Commentary—Much has been written regarding the equinoctial shadow on pages 204-205 and in the commentary of the seventh verse of this chapter. On the 205th page, it is stated that when the tangent of a place's latitude is divided by the gnomon, it gives the equinoctial shadow of that place. Therefore, it is necessary to state here that the value of the equinoctial shadow according to this verse is gross. Because on the day of the vernal equinox of Aries or Libra, when the shadow of the gnomon is measured at noon and the equinoctial shadow is known, the Sun is not exactly on the vernal equinox at noon but is some ahead or behind. The conjunction of the Sun coming exactly on the vernal equinox at noon happens after many years. On this day, the precession of the Sun changes by approximately one zodiac sign per hour. Therefore, one should know the precession of the Sun at noon by knowing the pure time calculation of the vernal equinox of Aries or Libra and after performing the correction, know the pure equinoctial shadow. The method of performing the correction will be shown in the next 14-15 verses.

From pictures 7 and 10 it is clear that the angular difference of any place from the equator on the north-south line is its latitude, and the angular difference of the place from the pole on the north-south line is its longitude. If the plane of the equator is extended towards the sky, this is called the prime vertical circle, and if the plane of the north-south line is extended in the sky, it is called the meridian circle. Similarly, when the line joining any place from the center of the Earth is raised, the point it reaches in the sky is called the astrolabe of that place. (14) To find the meridian altitude of the sun, multiply the shadow of a day's noon, which is also called the radius, by the shadow hypotenuse of the meridian and divide, and make an arc of the quotient, then the meridian altitude of the sun will be found. Sūrya Siddhānta - The circle drawn perpendicular to the horizon from a point (star, center of the sun, etc.) to which the science extends is called the Vertical Circle. The difference between that point and the x-coordinate from the x-coordinate is called the zenith distance of that point, and the difference from the horizon is called the altitude of that point. The prime vertical circle is also a vertical circle. But its special feature is that it is at the points east and west of the horizon. The meridian circle is also a vertical circle at the north and south points. Therefore, when the sun is on the meridian circle, the difference of the x-coordinate from it is its meridian altitude. If the sun is also on the equator circle, then this will be the same as the latitude. If the sun is not on the equator circle, then it will be either north or south of the equator circle. The difference of the sun from the equator circle at the meridian time is the sun's declination, which is called the north or south declination according to whether the sun is north or south of the sun's equator. Similarly, the sun can also be north or south of the x-coordinate. If the sun is north of the x-coordinate, the shadow will be towards the south, and the difference between the sun and the x-coordinate will be called the northern altitude. But if the sun is south of the x-coordinate, the shadow will be towards the north, and the altitude of the sun will be south. The rule given above for finding the portion only tells that how far the sun is from the vernal or autumnal equinox. If the sun is between three zodiac signs, i.e., between Aries and Pisces, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun from the vernal equinox, so this is the sine portion. If the sun is within three signs from the beginning of Cancer, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the autumnal equinox. But the autumnal equinox is 6 signs away from Aries, so the obtained portion has to be subtracted from 6 signs, then the sine portion of the sun from the vernal equinox is obtained. If the sun is between three signs from Libra, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the autumnal equinox, so 6 signs have to be added, then the sine portion of the sun from the vernal equinox is obtained. And if the sun is between three signs from Capricorn, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the vernal equinox. Therefore, by subtracting this portion from 12 signs, the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the vernal equinox (portion) is obtained.

Translation—When the shadow of the desired time is multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by the shadow hypotenuse, sine is obtained. Subtracting the square of sine from the square of the radius and taking the square root yields the gnomon. Multiplying the gnomon by the radius and dividing by the sine of colatitude gives the hole. Multiplying the hole by the sine of declination and dividing by the versed sine gives the sine of inclination. Subtracting this from the node gives the remainder, which is understood as the versed sine, and forming an arc from the versed sine body, the east or west time of day is known.

Scientific Commentary—The summary of these three shlokas is:—

(1) shadow x radius / shadow hypotenuse = sine (2) √(radius^2 - sine^2) = gnomon (3) gnomon x radius / sine of colatitude = hole (4) hole x radius / sine of declination = sine of inclination (5) node - sine of inclination = nto-versed sine

These are the opposites of the rules written in shlokas 34-35, so their derivation is the same. Yes, here, the value of the sine of the shadow, i.e., the sine of the ntaansh, should be known as in the rule mentioned in the 13th shloka. It has already been stated that the angle between the gnomon and the shadow hypotenuse is the ntaansh, so when the shadow is divided by the shadow hypotenuse, a decimal fraction * and when this result is multiplied by the radius, the value of the sine of the ntaansh of the arts is obtained.

Translation—On the day when the line of the tip of the shadow of the gnomon is to be drawn, determine three points of the shadow tip before and behind the meridian of that day. But the true Sun does not move with the same speed on the true Sun circle always. Sometimes its speed becomes fast and sometimes slow. Therefore, for this reason also the true Sun will not come to the true Sun meridian at the time when the mean Sun comes, as stated above. The true Sun and the mean Sun stay together only at the apogee and nadir of the true Sun circle (see pages 80-82). When the Sun moves ahead of the apogee, the daily motion of the true Sun is less than the daily motion of the mean Sun, so the true Sun falls behind the mean Sun, that is, the true Sun remains ahead of the mean Sun towards the east. Therefore, the true noon comes before the mean noon. For this reason also the time of the sun-dial remains ahead of the mean time. This condition remains until the Sun reaches the nadir. From here on, the motion of the true Sun is greater than the mean motion, so the true Sun remains ahead of the mean Sun towards the east. Therefore, the true noon is behind the mean noon, that is, the sundial remains slow compared to the mean time.

Due to these two reasons, that is, the movement on the true Sun circle and the difference in daily motion, there is some difference between the true time and the mean time. The time taken to subtract or add from the true time to find the mean time is called the 'Equation of Time'. It is also written as:-

Mean Time = True Time + Equation of Time*

* Venkatesh Vapu Ketkar has named it Udayantara in his astronomy (Jyotg. Ga. page 75)

As the distance from the earth increases, the atmosphere becomes thinner, so the total atmosphere is not homogeneous. When a ray coming from a celestial body enters the atmosphere, it first goes into a very thin layer, and as it approaches the earth, due to entering layers of less dense to more dense, it bends slightly towards the vertical and reaches the earth. Now in brief, it will be explained what our Acharyas have written about the arc:-

Bhaskaraacharya has written* that when the daily motion of a planet is divided by 15, the absolute arc length (horizon arc length) of that planet is obtained. The reason for this is explained:-

The circle of the sky that is touched by a horizontal (plane) touching any place on the earth is called the horizon circle of that place. This horizon circle divides the sphere of the sky into two parts. This horizon circle is called the sensible horizon circle. If a plane of sky is extended parallel to this sensible horizon circle towards another plane of sky passing through the center of the Earth, the circle that this plane cuts in the sky is called the true horizon circle of that place. In Figure 78, the position of the observer and the center of the Earth on the earth surface are shown. The line drawn from D touching the earth surface intersects the orbit of the Moon at point C and the orbit of the Sun at point S. Therefore, C, S are on the sensible horizon of the place. If a plane of sky is extended parallel to this, passing through another plane of sky which cuts the orbits of the Moon and the Sun at points C and S respectively, then this plane is called the true horizon of the place of D. It is apparent that when the Moon and the Sun or any other planet is on the true horizon of the place of D, at that time it is in the plane B C S which is below the sensible horizon of D, so it will not be seen by the observer. In such a situation, the magnitude with which the planet remains below the sensible horizon is C or S (which is equal to B D, i.e., the semi-diameter of the Earth).

Many texts of ancient literature have been published on behalf of Dr. Ratnakumari Swadhyay Sansthan—the texts of Swami Satyaprakash and Dr. Usha Jyotishmati, such as Bakhashali-Manuscript, Shulba-Sutras (in Sanskrit and English). In this tradition, we are publishing the Scientific Commentary of Sūrya Siddhānta by Swargiya Shri Mahabir Prasad Srivastava. We are extremely grateful to Chaudhary Sahab. We have already published the first volume in March 1982, which includes Chapter on Mean Motions, Chapter on True Positions, and Chapter on the Three Problems. This second volume has 11 chapters. To know how an eclipse occurs between the sun and the moon, some properties of light are first necessary. Therefore, these will be considered briefly first. It is everyone's experience that in the light of a lamp at night, the shadow cast on the wall of an object is somewhere light and somewhere deep. The deep shadow is in the middle and the light shadow surrounds the deep shadow. If the object is near the wall, the deep shadow is large and the light shadow is small. As the object moves further away from the wall, the extension of the shadow increases, but the deep shadow decreases and the light shadow increases. If the object is smaller than the lamp, there will also be a situation where the deep shadow does not fall at all, only the light shadow will be seen on the wall.


## Source page 467

Yes, if the object is larger than the lamp, a deep shadow will always fall on the wall.

The part of the wall where the deep shadow falls, no part of the lamp's light reaches that part, but in the light shadow, some part of the lamp's light must reach. If an insect is in the deep shadow on the wall, it will not see the lamp at all, but in the light shadow, it will surely see some part of the lamp. This can be tested as follows:-

Keep a lamp or candle lit. Place a pencil, bullet, or any object smaller than the lamp a short distance away, standing or hanging. Hold a thin paper in your hand in such a way that both deep and light shadows of the pencil fall on it. Make a hole with a needle in the deep shadow and see if the lamp can see or not. The lamp will not see. Make a hole by piercing in the light shadow and see. Some part of the lamp will be seen.

From geometry, it can be known where the deep shadow will fall and where the light shadow will fall. It is also possible to determine the extent of these. To know how eclipses happen in the Sun and Moon, the mathematics of the deep and light shadows has to be done, so it is necessary to think about this well. Further, the deep shadow will be called shadow and the light shadow will be called umbra.

Suppose R is a luminous body and C is an opaque body. Both bodies are spherical. The rays of light from R spread in all directions, but the rays that fall on body C cannot proceed further than it. If lines are drawn that touch both these bodies, they will move forward, intersecting each other at point T. It will be of the shape of a cone. This will be the boundary of the shadow formed by body C. Shadows will not fall above, below, to the sides. (See Figure 60).

The lines that touch both these bodies and meet at point T form the boundary of the umbra.

If a sheet (screen) is kept in shadow in such a way that it is at a right angle to the line joining the centers of the r and c bodies, then the diameter of the circle of shadow that will be formed on this sheet will be ch cha, and the diameter of the circle of the umbra will be u u, which includes the diameter of the shadow (see figure 61). If a hole is made at a point p in the segment u ch and the light-emitting body is seen through this hole, then the upper part of the body which is above the point p will be seen. This point p a

All these views can be seen by experiment. A round lamp, a ball, and wooden pegs are sufficient for these three things. The round lamp should be understood in place of the body and the ball in place of the peg. This experiment can be easily done in any place during a dark night.

Since the Earth is much larger than the Moon, the entire Earth cannot fall in shadow or penumbra. The inhabitants of the part of the Earth that falls in shadow do not see the Sun at all. The planimetric shape of the sun does not increase or decrease according to the apparent motion; yes, the artistic or angular shape certainly changes, which has been well done in the Chapter on True Positions on pages 84-86. Here, although the magnitude of the mean diameter and the apparent diameter is stated in the calculations, it should be understood as angular because this is the meaning derived from what Bhaskaraacharya ji1 has written about the method of knowing this. Bhaskaraacharya ji says that on the day when the apparent or true motion of the sun is similar to the mean motion, on that day, in the rising time, take two sticks of the same length and join their two ends, placing eyes at two original places, and extend the image of the sun in such a way that the forward ends of these sticks touch the north and south edges of the image. In this situation, fasten the ends of the sticks in such a way that there is no difference in the distance of the forward ends. Now measure the distance of these ends with the same unit with which the length of the sticks was measured. This difference, if it is equal to some number of units, will be the diameter of the sun's image in the artistic sense. According to Bhaskaraacharya ji, this diameter is 32'31''33''. Multiply the sine of the netaṃśa of the circumposition of the chhaya graha by the sine of the latitude of the desired place, and divide the product by the radius of the ahoratravritta of the planet, and make the quotient an arc. (25) Adding 60 degrees to the sine portion of the planet, the resulting portion is obtained by taking the inclination (according to chapter on true positions verse 28) by multiplying it by the sine of the ultimate revolution (of the ahoratravritta) and dividing by the radius. This quotient is called the inclination. This will be to the north or south. If the directions of the axis and the inclination are the same, add them, and if they are different, subtract them. Calculation of the night-time—

To know the time of the moon, one must first know the time of the sun. In the meridian time, the sun remains on the meridian circle, and in the midnight time as well, it remains on the meridian circle below the horizon, therefore the center of the Earth's shadow remains on the meridian circle in the midnight time because the center of the Earth's shadow remains at exactly 180 degrees from the sun. Therefore, the time of the center of the Earth's shadow in the midnight time is zero. If it is known how much before or after midnight the time of touch is, then it is easily known how far east or west the time of the center of the Earth's shadow is in the time of touch. During a lunar eclipse, the moon is very close to the Earth's shadow, and it is known that the moon is at what distance from the Earth's shadow, therefore the time of the moon can be easily known.

By doing this, the middle time of the eclipse is known.

At the time when the moon, while moving towards the east, becomes equal to the portion of the sun, at that time the end of the new moon occurs. This is called the mathematical proven new moon end. When the sun is to the east of the three-fold ascendant, the moon, due to declination, hangs to the east and becomes in front of the sun before the new moon. Therefore, as much as the relative declination of both, the end of the true new moon occurs earlier. For this reason, in the first half of the shloka, it is said to subtract the declination from the mathematically proven time. Conversely, when the sun is to the west of the three-fold ascendant, the moon does not appear in front of the sun even in the mathematically proven new moon time because, due to declination, it hangs a little lower towards the west. Therefore, as much declination occurs at this time, the true new moon time is behind. That is why adding this declination results in the true new moon.

## Source page 538

It is clear that at the time of touch, the portion of the Sun or Moon will be greater than the portion of the Sun or Moon in the mean time and less in the time of salvation because the ecliptic is the highest point of the declination above the horizon, and the Sun and Moon rise respectively, meaning their portion decreases, so the portion of the time of touch is greater than the portion of the mean time, and the portion of the time of salvation is less than the portion of the mean time. But if both touch and salvation are in the western hemisphere, then at the time of touch, the portion of the Sun will be less than the mean time portion, and the portion in the time of salvation will be greater than the mean time portion because the Sun or Moon descend in the western hemisphere, so their portion increases.

Adding the difference between the time of touch and the mean time of the latitudes to the mean position of the anterior hemisphere gives the true position of touch because the position calculated first is according to the latitude of the mean time, but the latitude in the time of touch is some more, so due to this, the Moon hangs a little lower, i.e., towards the east, so the touch is seen a little earlier, meaning the value of the position increases. But in the time of salvation (being in the anterior hemisphere), the latitude remains less compared to the mean time, so adding the difference between these two also gives the true position of salvation because when the latitude in the time of salvation is less, the Moon does not hang as much towards the east as in the mean time, so it remains for a longer time in front of the Sun and the position of salvation also increases.

Due to the obliquity in the western skull, the moon hangs towards the west, which causes a some delay in it coming in front of the sun because the motion of the moon is always towards the east and east, and due to the obliquity, it seems as if it is also going towards the west. For this reason, the time of eclipse is some behind the time of the mathematical amāvasyānta time. However, the lunar portion of the touch time is less than the mean time because the eclipse occurs some time after the touch time, and in this time, due to the daily motion of the earth or the flow of air due to the ancient view, the sun and moon all appear below. Therefore, the touch time obliquity in the western skull is less than the mean obliquity due to the lesser portion of the lunar portion, which has the effect that the eclipse does not take as much delay in touching as it does in the mean time, that is, due to the lesser obliquity at the time of touch.

In the second case, that is, in a lunar eclipse, one will have to consider how much of the sun is eclipsed at the time of sunset and how many eclipses have touched it before. For this action as well, the same verses will have to be used.
