Scientific Commentary—in these verses, the method of knowing the distance and the direction in which the center of the observer is located at the touch, mean, and culmination of the reception, assuming the received image is fixed, is explained with the help of trigonometry. In a lunar eclipse, the moon is the received and the Earth's shadow is the observer. In a solar eclipse, the sun is the received and the moon is the observer. Now, the explanation of each method in the order of the verses is given:—

Verse 2—It is stated in verses 24-25 and pages 475-480 that the subtension is and how the knowledge of the ecliptic is obtained from it. It is also stated there that when the sine of the subtension is divided by 70, its sine value comes in angulas. Thus, the value of the radius is approximately 46 angulas because the radius is 3438 arts, which when divided by 70 gives a remainder of 46·1, which should be understood as 46 in integers. Therefore, in this verse, the method of drawing the circle with the semi-diameter of 46 angulas is explained. The line indicating the subtension can be easily drawn from this circle. Bhaskaracharya and other Acharyas have not stated the rule for drawing the semi-diameter circle. They have only written that on the circle of conjunction, the angles for east, west, north, and south should be made according to the direction for the magnitude of the subtension.

Verse 3—In this verse, the discussion is about the drawing of the circle of the image of the planet in which an eclipse occurs, that is, the circle of the apparent image. However, it is not made clear what its magnitude should be. If one considers one angula of 70 degrees, then the circle of the conjunction and the apparent image will be very small because the diameter of the apparent image circle is less than 16 degrees or one-fourth of an angula, and the diameter of the conjunction circle is about 1 angula. Therefore, considering one angula of 70 degrees will not be convenient for these circles. In such a situation, the angula discussed in the 26th verse of the chapter on lunar eclipse is necessary.

The reason for this is clear. The moon moves towards the east in the sky while revolving around the Earth, so at the time it begins to enter the shadow of the Earth, its eastern part enters the shadow first. Similarly, the posterior part of the lunar image is separated from the shadow at the time of the moon; but in a solar eclipse, the lunar image moves from the posterior to the anterior of the sun's image and covers the sun's image, so at the time of contact, the posterior part of the sun's image begins to be covered and at the time of eclipse, the anterior part of the sun's image is separated from the lunar image.

What is the color of the image of the observer--

> अर्धादूनं च धूम्रं स्यात्कृष्णमर्धाधिकं भवेत् ।

(23) When less than half of the lunar image is covered, the covered part has a smoky color. When more than half is covered, the covered part appears black. When a large part of the lunar image is covered and only a little remains, the color of the covered part is black with a reddish tinge. But


## Source page 585

The color of the total eclipse is reddish-brown. (In a solar eclipse, the color of the part of the sun being eclipsed is always black.)

Scientific Commentary—As long as the moonlight remains bright, the eclipsed part appears smoky or black in comparison. But when only a small part of the moon remains, its light becomes without heat. Therefore, the color of the eclipsed part also appears somewhat red. The reason for this redness is that the subtle light of the sun, refracting through the atmosphere, falls on the lunar image, so some redness appears on the black eclipsed part. At the time when the entire lunar image falls into shadow, the lunar image does not appear black but brownish with redness. The reason for this is also the refracted light of the sun, which falls on the moon by passing through the Earth's atmosphere. If there were no atmosphere, the color of the eclipsed part of the moon would always be black, as the color of the eclipsed sun.

Due to the rotation of the atmosphere, sometimes another astonishing phenomenon is also seen. When an eclipse occurs during the rising or setting time, the eclipsed moon is seen in the presence of the shining sun, where one side of the moon is eclipsed and the other side of the sun keeps the Earth illuminated by its brightness. Such phenomena were seen in the years 1666, 1668, and 1750 AD.

Scientific Commentary—The two rules explained from the latter part of the 3rd verse to the end of the 6th verse are very similar to the rules of "time and distance" in arithmetic. An example of this is—a passenger train started from Prayag towards Patna at 6 o'clock in the morning at a speed of 25 miles per hour, and the mail train started in the same direction at 8 o'clock at a speed of 40 miles per hour. Then tell us where and when both will meet?

The same method is used to calculate the conjunction of the planets. In such questions, it is first necessary to know at what time the mail train started, what the difference was between the passenger train and that time, then it is necessary to know how long it will take for the mail train to cover this difference by moving 15 miles more per hour. Here, 15 miles is the difference in the hourly speeds of both trains because both trains are moving in the same direction.

If the passenger train starts from Prayag towards Patna and the mail train starts from Patna towards Prayag at 6 o'clock, then by adding the speeds of both and dividing this sum by the distance between Prayag and Patna, the time at which both trains will meet will be known. Here, the speeds are added because both trains are moving towards each other, so their speed of meeting is equal to the sum of their speeds.

(11) In finding the rising and setting of the planet in the sum of the constellation and the planet, before knowing the elongation of the moon, this procedure should be performed. (23) Whether Venus is to the north or to the south, it is often victorious. Similarly, the conjunction of the five luminaries with the Moon should be achieved.

Scientific Commentary—from the table of the smallest and greatest apparent sizes of five star planets it is revealed that the smallest apparent size of Venus is greater than the smallest apparent sizes of Mars and Mercury, therefore at the time of their conjunction, Venus is more victorious due to its greater luminosity and bulk. At the time when the apparent size of Mars is supreme, it is 180 degrees ahead of the Sun. In such a situation, the conjunction of Venus with it cannot happen; the conjunction of Venus and Mars can only happen when Mars is also near the Sun. In such a situation, the apparent size of Mars will always be smaller than the apparent size of Venus. Therefore, Venus is always more luminous and victorious than Mars and Mercury. Yes, when Venus is in conjunction with Jupiter or Saturn, then Venus is smaller than them for some time before setting in the east and rising in the west. Therefore, it can be said that it is defeated by Saturn or Jupiter, but such a state occurs very rarely. That is why it is said in this verse that Venus is usually victorious.

## Source page 633

Scientific Commentary—by multiplying the self-elongation of each star by 10 according to the first verse, the self-elongation art of the star will be obtained. By adding this to the courses of the past constellations, the pole of that star will be known. For example, the self-elongation of the Ashvini star is 48, multiplying it by 10 gives its self-elongation as 480 degrees. The Ashvini star is in the first constellation named Ashvini, so the past constellation is zero, hence the pole of the Ashvini star is 480 degrees or 8 arc minutes. Similarly, the self-elongation of the Rohini star is 570 degrees in arc minutes. The first three constellations of Rohini are Ashvini, Bharani, Krittika, so their elongation is 3 X 800 arc minutes because one constellation is equal to 800 arc minutes (see Chapter on True Positions verse 64). Therefore, the pole of the Rohini star = 570 + 3 + 800 arc minutes = 570 X 2400 arc minutes = 2670 arc minutes = 46 degrees 30 arc minutes.

Similarly, the declination of each star can be known. This is a characteristic of the elongations of the Uttaraashadha, Abhijita, Shravana, and Dhanishtha stars, so their declinations are stated as below:-

The star of Uttaraashadha is at half of the Purvashadha constellation, that is, at 400 arc minutes of the Purvashadha constellation. There are 16 constellations from the first Ashvini to the root of Purvashadha, whose elongations are equal to 16 X 800 arc minutes = 15200 arc minutes. Therefore, the declination of Uttaraashadha is 400 + 15200 arc minutes = 15600 arc minutes = 260 degrees.

The Abhijita star is stated at the end of Purvashadha, so its declination is 260 degrees + 400 arc minutes, that is, 266 degrees 40 arc minutes.

The pole of the Shravana star is at the end of the Uttaraashadha constellation. One constellation = 13 degrees 20 arc minutes. The end of the Purvashadha constellation is at 266 degrees 40 arc minutes, so the pole of the Shravana star at the end of Uttaraashadha is 280 degrees.

The Pole Star is at the end of the third quadrant of the Navagraha constellation. The three quadrants of the constellation are 600 degrees. Or they are equal to 10 degrees. Therefore, the pole of Dhinishtha is 280+10=260 degrees.

The deflection is given in degrees, so there is no need to write more on this.

Scientific Commentary—There are 5 stars in the Rohini constellation whose shapes are like a cart or the letter V of the English alphabet. The southern deviation of the northernmost star among these five is approximately 2 degrees 35 arc. This star is called Apellan star nowadays. And the southern deviation of the star conjunct Rohini is 5 arc 32 arc. The planet whose southern deviation or deviation falls between these two limits falls within the shadow of Rohini. This is called the penetration of the shadow of Rohini. It is apparent that the deviation of the planet depends on its node. The Moon completes one revolution in 18 years. In this one revolution, the Moon only passes through 5,6 years of shadow. If the southern deviation of the Moon is more than 2 degrees 35 arc and less than 5 arc 32 arc and at that time it is in the Rohini constellation, then it will certainly be within the shadow of Rohini, therefore the Moon will have the Rohini-shadow-penetration. Now it is to see that at the time the Moon is in the Rohini constellation, its southern deviation is less than 2 degrees 35 arc.

In page 75 of the Chapter on Mean Motions it is stated that the ultimate displacement of the Moon is 5 degrees 8 nakshas 42 vikalas. This means that when the Moon is 60 degrees ahead of Rahu, its south is 5 degrees 8 nakshas and 42 vikalas, and when it is 60 degrees ahead of Ketu, its south is the same. But when it is on Rahu or Ketu, its south is zero. Therefore, based on the verses of the Chapter on True Positions 28 and figure 25, it can be easily known that the south of the Moon is more than 2 degrees 35 nakshas. In this figure, if we assume the Moon's orbit, the ecliptic, the position of Rahu, the position of the Moon, the Moon's south, and the Moon's ultimate displacement, then the relation between the Moon and the ecliptic can be easily known. Here, if we assume that the Moon and the ecliptic are 2 degrees 35 nakshas, then


That is, when the moon is one amount ahead of its node, then its shadow is more than 2 degrees 35 arcminutes. But Rohini is to the south of the ecliptic and its polar-facing portion according to Sūrya Siddhānta is 46 degrees 30 arcminutes and according to Shankar Balakrishna Dikshit is 47 degrees 37 arcminutes and the Kadamba-facing portion


## Source page 645

From the calculation of Sūrya Siddhānta, there are 48 degrees 6 kala and Shankar Balakrishna Dikshit has 45 degrees 57 kala from the calculation. Therefore, if the portion of the star of Rohini facing Kadamba is assumed to be 46 degrees, then at the time when the portion of the moon is the same, the Rohini-Shakta-Bheda may occur if its south shadow is more than 2 degrees 35 kala. In such a situation, the moon should be at least 1 rashi ahead of Ketu, that is, the Rohini-Shakta-Bheda can only occur when the portion of Ketu is at least 16 degrees.

From the above calculation it is proved that when the Moon is 1 sign ahead of Ketu, its southern deviation is 2°35' art. After this, its southern deviation increases to 5°8' art. At that time it is 3 signs ahead of Ketu. Then its southern deviation begins to decrease and when it is 5 signs ahead of Ketu or 1 sign behind Rahu, its southern deviation is not less than 2°35' art. Within this limit, the Moon passes the shadow of Rohini. However, it is proved above that when Ketu's portion is 16 art, that is when Ketu is at the 16th degree of Aries, if the Moon's southern deviation is 2°35' art, then there will be a Rohini-shkat-bhed. After this, even when Ketu moves backward due to its retrograde motion, the Moon will still pass the shadow of Rohini because at that time its southern deviation in Rohini constellation will be more than 2°35' art. Thus, until Ketu moves 4 signs behind the 16th degree of Aries, the Moon's southern deviation in Rohini constellation will remain less than 2°35' art. This means that when Ketu comes to the 16th degree of Aries, the beginning of the Moon's Rohini-shkat bhed will occur, and until it does not come to the 16th degree of Sagittarius, the Moon's Rohini-shkat-bhed in Rohini constellation will be there. However, it remains 6 signs ahead of Rahu-Ketu. Therefore, it can also be said that until it remains in the range from the 16th degree of Gemini to the 16th degree of Libra, the Moon's Rohini-shkat-bhed occurs.

Similarly, the Rohini shadow-difference of other planets can also be calculated. Saturn's true shadow-difference is 2 degrees 26 arcminutes 36 arcseconds, so Saturn's Rohini-shadow-difference is also considered impossible.

## Source page 663

Which time should one see the sky picture? If one needs to use the sky picture from any other date of the month, then it should be kept in mind that the view seen at 10 o'clock on the 1st date of the month will be seen 4 minutes before 10 o'clock on the 2nd date, 4x2=8 minutes before 10 o'clock on the 3rd date, 4x7=28 minutes before the 8th date (i.e., one week later), and 15x4=60 minutes or 1 hour before on the 16th date, meaning it will be seen at 6 o'clock. The reason for this is that the Earth moves forward by 1 degree in the orbit of the Sun during the day and night, causing the Sun to appear one degree towards the east of the stars. Therefore, the Sun takes 4 minutes longer to come into the meridian circle each day, or the Sun's declination increases by approximately 4 minutes per day. However, the celestial time for which the sky picture is made is fixed, so the time at which the sky is seen on any day is seen 4 minutes before at the same time on the next day (see pages 463-466). The direct rule is that the view shown in the sky picture appears in the sky at the same time as the celestial time of the sky picture is earlier or later than the Sun's declination at noon. For example, on the 1st date of Vaishakh, the noon declination of the Sun is approximately 1 hour 26 minutes, and the celestial time of the sky picture of Jyeshtha is 10 hours 30 minutes, which is 12 hours 1 minute behind the noon declination. Therefore, the sky picture of Jyeshtha will be seen at 12:01 at night on the 1st date of Vaishakh. But the reason why 11:56 is mentioned in the 6th column is that 12 hours 1 minute is in the celestial time and 11 hours 56 minutes is in the Sun-dial time for Savan. Because it has been stated that the Savan day is approximately 4 minutes larger than the celestial day (see pages 337-36), the 6 hours of celestial time are the same as 5 hours 56 minutes of the Savan time.

According to this rule, if you wish to see all the stars in the sky on the first day of the month of Magha in the same night, you can see them easily. On this date, the stars set before five and a half o'clock of the sun in the directions of the lines connecting Bombay and Jagannath Puri, that is, in all of North India. Therefore, the stars in the sky become clearly visible at the time of 6 o'clock in the evening. On this date, the obliquity of the meridian sun is 16 hours and 42 minutes, so from noon

If you look at the sky at 12 o'clock at night, 6 hours behind, then the Nakshatra time will be approximately 7 hours 42 minutes, which can be useful for the sky picture of Phalgun month because the sky picture of Phalgun month is the one when the Nakshatra time is 7 hours 30 minutes. Simple description of the diagram—the round line drawn in the diagram is the horizon of 25 degrees latitude, so it is usually found with the horizon of Prayag or Kashi. A sign of wealth is shown in the center in this manner. From this, the point in the sky is revealed which is just above the head at 25 degrees latitude. This is called khswastik or khmadhya. North, South, East, West and the directions between them are visible near the round line. The straight line seen from North to South is the meridian circle. The sun remains on this line at noon. The crooked line seen from East to West is the equator. On the days of spring equinox and autumn equinox, the sun appears on this and rises exactly in the east and sets exactly in the west. There is another line that cuts the equator, which is called the ecliptic. The sun is seen moving on this every day. In reality, this is the path of our Earth on which the sun travels and completes one revolution throughout the year. This path is of great importance. The moon and planets revolve around it in the sky.

### Sky Picture of Margashir Month

In this month the sky remains very clear. The dust of the months of Vaishakh and Jyeshtha and the clouds of Shravan and Bhadrapada are not seen anywhere, nor does the fog of Magha and Phagun reach the vision. Therefore, there is both knowledge and mental delight from the sky-picture of this month. In the sky of this month, many new stars and star groups are seen in the east direction, which have also been discussed in many places in ancient literature.

North—the stars of the small saptarṣi hang near the horizon. At this time, the Pole Star is at the very top among them. Three faint stars of Cygnus are seen spreading towards the west above the small saptarṣi. As much above the horizon as the Pole Star is, the constellation of Cassiopeia is seen in the shape of the English letter M. Its four large stars pass the meridian circle and go towards the west

Above the swan are many dim stars. The northern stars are called Pushyanakshatra and the southern stars are called Ashlesha Nakshatra. The Cancer constellation is also here. All the dim stars between Punarvasu and Magha can be said to be in the Cancer constellation.

## Source page 677

### Chapter on the Right Ascension

### (Brief Description)

[1 verse—The idea that planets and stars become invisible due to coming near the sun. 2-3 verses—The direction of the rising and setting of planets. 4-5 verses—The method of knowing the occultation of planets. 6-6 verses—The ultimate occultation of planets. 10-11 verses—The method of knowing how many days are remaining or have passed for a rising or setting at a certain time. 12-15 verses—Which star has what ultimate occultation. 16-17 verses—The method of knowing the day of visibility or disappearance of a star. 18 verses—The names of those stars that are never invisible]

In this chapter, it is explained when the rising and setting of planets and stars occur and how they are known. Here, the meaning of rising and setting is different from the ordinary meanings of rising and setting. Generally, when the sun, moon, etc., come above the eastern horizon, they are considered to have risen, and when they go below the western horizon, they are considered to have set. This is due to the daily motion of the Earth, which the old Acharyas called Pravah-gati. Besides this, when planets, the moon, or stars come very close to the sun, so that they come above the eastern horizon almost before sunrise and below the western horizon almost after sunset, they are also considered to have set. In such a situation, they cannot be seen due to the intense light of the sun. The time from which they become invisible because they come near the sun is considered as setting, and the time when they are so far from the sun that they begin to be seen a little before sunrise or a little after sunset is considered as rising. Similar discussions of rising and setting are mentioned in this right. Western astrologers call this heliacal rising and setting.

Purpose of the chapter—

> अथोदयास्तमययोः परिज्ञानं प्रकीर्त्यते ।

> दिवकरकराक्रान्त मूर्तीनामल्पतेजसाम् ॥१॥

Another point is worth considering in this regard. From what has been said so far about the rising and setting of planets, it has become clear that they are said to have set only when they come so close to the sun that they cannot be seen due to the twilight of morning or evening. However, the intensity and limit of twilight are not the same in all seasons and places. Anyone can experience that the limit of twilight increases in the winter days and decreases in the summer days. The reason for this is that twilight is related to the portion of the sun below the horizon, which depends on the sun's declination and the latitude of the ecliptic (see page 261 sutra 1). It has been proven by experience that as long as the sun is not more than 180 degrees below the horizon, some part of its light still returns to the Earth through the atmosphere. From the time of the sun's setting until the time when it does not go more than 18 degrees below the horizon, when dim light is seen, that is called twilight.

Translation—(6) If the directions of the Sun and the Moon are the same, then find the difference of their sines, and if they are different, then find the sum. The direction in which the Sun is, that direction should also understand this difference or sum; that is, if the Moon is south of the Sun, then understand the direction of the difference or sum as south, and if it is north, then understand it as north. (7) Multiply this sum or difference by the instantaneous shadow hypotenuse of the Moon. If the direction is north, then subtract this product from the product of 12 and the sine of latitude, and if it is south, then add it. (8) Divide this remainder or sum by the sine of colatitude and consider the result as the length of the desired direction. The result obtained by taking the square root of the sum of the squares of the length and the latitude is the hypotenuse. This hypotenuse is the formulaic or linear difference between the Sun and the Moon.

Scientific Commentary—When the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon are the same, then the nodes and apogees exist, that is, when the distances of the Sun and the Moon from the equator are the same, then the nodes and apogees occur. But even when the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon are the same, both can be North or both South; or one North and the other South. Now we have to see when this condition occurs. When the Sun is on the equator, its revolution is zero. This phenomenon occurs twice a year—on the vernal equinox and the autumnal equinox. From Aries to Cancer, the revolution of the Sun increases from zero to about 23 degrees 27 signs. It begins to decrease from Cancer and decreases to Libra, becoming zero again. From Libra, the revolution is South, and it increases to Capricorn, becoming 23 degrees 27 signs. From Capricorn to Aries, it decreases and becomes zero. When the Sun moves ahead from Capricorn, it appears to move towards the North on the horizon at the time of rising or setting, and this motion is seen up to Cancer. That is why the time from the Aries equinox to the Cancer equinox is called Uttarayana. But after the Cancer equinox, the Sun appears to move towards the South on the horizon, that is why the time from the Cancer equinox to the Capricorn equinox is called Dakshinayana. The Moon also, like the Sun, remains in Uttarayana for half a month and Dakshinayana for half a month in its revolution of almost one month, but because its orbit is somewhat different from the ecliptic and due to the self-retrograde motion of its orbit and the ecliptic at the points of intersection with Rahu and Ketu, it is somewhat difficult to fix the time of its Uttarayana and Dakshinayana. But in broad terms, there is no harm in saying that when the Moon comes near the Capricorn sign, then it is Uttarayana, and when it comes near the Cancer sign, then it is Dakshinayana because the angle between the lunar orbit and the ecliptic, that is the Moon's true position, is only about 506. From Figure 120 it is clear that when the Moon remains in an odd position, i.e., in V or Shu, then for the transit or occultation, the Sun should be in the Shu or U position in sequence. It is also clear that the revolution of the Sun or Moon increases in odd positions and decreases in mean positions. Therefore, when the Moon is in an odd position and the Sun is in a mean position, the revolution of the Moon continues to increase and the revolution of the Sun continues to decrease. Therefore, the gross time of the nodal period extracted from the sixth verse, if the revolution of the Moon is more than the revolution of the Sun at that time, the revolution of the Moon will increase and the revolution of the Sun will decrease. Therefore, both revolutions have become equal before this time and the nodal period has passed. Conversely, if the revolution of the Moon is less than the revolution of the Sun, due to the revolution of the Moon continuing to increase, the time is coming when both revolutions will be equal and then the nodal period will occur. Similarly, when the Moon is in mean positions, the Sun will be in odd positions. In such a situation, the revolution of the Moon will decrease and the revolution of the Sun will continue to increase. Therefore, if the Moon's revolution is more, it will become equal to the decreasing revolution of the Sun and will come after the time extracted from the nodal period verse 6. But if the revolution of the Moon is less, then the nodal period should be considered as passed.

Sūrya Siddhānta – in these six shlokas there is a very clear description of the position of four cities located on the Tropic of Cancer. These cities are in the fourth quadrant of the Earth's circumference from each other, that is, they are separated by 60 degrees and North Meru (North Pole) is also at the same distance from them to the north. The directions of these cities are considered from the Indian subcontinent. Lanka is at the Tropic of Cancer of the south of the Indian subcontinent, and its position should be considered as the longitude of Ujjain according to the 62nd shloka of the Chapter on Mean Motions (madhyamādhikāra) (page 65). The longitude of Ujjain from Greenwich is approximately 76 degrees. Therefore, if Lanka is considered at this longitude and the Tropic of Cancer, there is a sea here nowadays. The place 60 degrees east of this is at a longitude of 166 degrees east of Greenwich. Therefore, the place of Yamakoti city is also a sea nowadays. Since there are no land names on the Tropic of Cancer 60 degrees west of Lanka or 14 degrees west of Greenwich, the location of Romak city also cannot be determined. This Romak city would have been about 50 miles south of the Free Town of Western Africa nowadays. Similarly, Siddapuri would have been more than 1000 miles south of Mexico.

If the existence of these four spheres ever existed, then that time would be very ancient because nowadays the difference has become so much that there is no mark of that time in the present. It is also possible that the existence of these four spheres remained only in the poet's imagination and this has been described in figurative language that these four places on the equator are such that when noon is in Lanka, then sunrise is in Romaka, midnight in Siddhapuri, and sunset in Yamakoti.

It is clear that when the sun is on the cross on the equator, then at noon there is no shadow of any standing object. There are the north and south poles on the horizon of this line, so the height of the pole star here is zero. Therefore, the latitude is also zero. For this reason, the equator is called the meridian country. Its further and clearer description is in the next three verses.

Sūrya Siddhānta is stated to be emerging from the middle of the Earth on both sides, therefore it should be understood as the axis of the Earth whose northern end is the North Pole.

Scientific Commentary—Here it is stated that the North and South Poles have the Pole Star in the middle, which is on the horizon of the meridian. It can be estimated from this that when the Sūrya Siddhānta was said in ancient times, there were two Pole Stars. It can also be said that just as there is a star in the middle of the North Pole, a star was also understood to be in the middle of the South Pole. But it is certain that the star seen in the middle of the North Pole at this time was not at this place in ancient times because its position is also changing due to precession (see pages 240-42). Therefore, the Pole Stars described here are the positions of the celestial poles which are in the middle of the North and South Poles. They have no eternal relationship with any star. Verse 45 is of great importance. It is stated that when the sun is at the beginning of the Aries sign, the gods see it first, that is, when the sun rises for the inhabitants of the North Pole, and when it is at the beginning of the Libra sign, the demons see it first, that is, when it rises for the inhabitants of the South Pole. It appears that the beginning of the Aries sign should be understood as the place where the ecliptic and the tropics are in conjunction and where the sun becomes in the northern hemisphere. This place is called the Vernal Equinox point. Similarly, the beginning point of Libra is the Autumnal Equinox point where the sun becomes in the southern hemisphere. When the sun comes to the tropics at the beginning of Aries, sunrise occurs for the northern pole dwellers, and they see the sun equally for 6 months. This time is called the day of the gods. And the night of the demons because until the sun is seen by the northern pole dwellers, it remains invisible for the southern pole dwellers and there is night. When the sun reaches the beginning of Libra, sunset occurs at the northern pole and sunrise at the southern pole. For 6 months from this time, the sun is seen equally at the southern pole and there is the day of the month. These characteristics on the northern and southern poles and the equator occur because the poles are 60 degrees apart from the equator (see page 62).

Therefore, the inhabitants of the North Pole see the gods on the horizon and the inhabitants of the South Pole see the demons. However, because the sun's motion is towards the North, it appears to rise for the gods and set for the demons. That is, from this day the day of the gods and the night of the demons begins. This position of the sun, that is the Vernal Equinox point, is called the beginning of Aries. After this, the sun moves towards the North every day. When it reaches 60 degrees from the Vernal Equinox point, its northward movement stops. On this day, the gods see it at its highest point. This height is like the sun's ultimate revolution. Therefore, on this day is the noon of the gods and the midnight of the demons. From the Vernal Equinox point up to 60 degrees, there are three zodiacs: Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. When the sun passes from the beginning of Cancer to Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, and reaches the beginning of Libra, it comes onto the ecliptic. At this time, the gods see it setting. Therefore, from this time the night of the gods and the day of the demons begins. This position of the sun is called the Autumnal Equinox point, and this day is also called the Equinox day. After this, as long as the sun remains in the Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius zodiacs, there is the afternoon of the demons and the pre-night of the gods. When the sun reaches the Capricorn zodiac, it is the midnight of the gods and the noon of the demons. When the sun is in the Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces zodiacs, it is the afternoon of the demons. In this way, the time taken for one revolution of the sun is the same time for one night of the gods or one day of the demons. But the day of the gods is the night of the demons, and the night of the gods is the day of the demons.

From this description it is clear that the beginning of the zodiac signs such as Aries, Taurus, etc., is considered from the vernal equinox, not from the retrograde Aries which is currently 23 degrees ahead of the vernal equinox and which is always moving further ahead of the vernal equinox. This difference is called precession angle. More than 1400 years ago, when the vernal equinox and retrograde Aries were together, the position of Aries was the same as what is called retrograde Aries today, but this is not the case now. For this reason, two schools have emerged among astrologers today, the siderealists and the retrogradists. Those called siderealists consider the vernal equinox as the beginning of Aries. But the retrogradists consider retrograde Aries as the starting point of the zodiac signs.

From this, all objects in the sky appear to move from east to west. From this, the origin of day and night occurs. With the second motion, the Earth completes one orbit of the Sun in a year, which causes the origin of the seasons, and in the sky, the Sun appears to move from west to east while orbiting the Earth in a year. This motion is called the annual motion of the Earth. Both these motions occur simultaneously in the Earth, as a ball thrown upwards dances on its axis and changes its position, or as a top played by boys dances and changes its position.

Therefore, from this pendulum experiment, not only the motion of the Earth will not be known, but its direction will also be known.

Foucault performed this experiment in Paris in the year 1851 or 1608. He hung his pendulum from the dome of a large building named Panthéon. The wire was 200 feet long and the weight of the sphere was about 1 mina (80 pounds). At the time the pendulum swung, the needle that came out from below the sphere continued to make the mark of its swinging on the plane, and it was seen that the plane of the sand was rotating in the direction of the apse, that is, from right to left, from west to east.

Two things must be kept with great care in this experiment. The pendulum should remain swinging for as long as its string is long, otherwise it will stop quickly by rubbing against the air with its high speed. Secondly, it is good if its sphere is as heavy as possible because this reduces the effects of hanging defects and air friction greatly.

The line formed by the pole of the pendulum in the northern hemisphere rotates in the adverse direction of the clock, similarly here there is a direction of rotation of the latitudes. But in the southern hemisphere, the line formed by the pole of the pendulum and the direction of the latitudes rotate in the favorable direction of the clock. The winds that blow from the equator towards the pole move towards the east in the northern hemisphere, i.e., to the right, and in the southern hemisphere also towards the east, i.e., they turn to their left. The reason for this and what else could it be?


## Source page 791

it is that when the air above the equator is warm and light, it rises, so to fill its place, the cold air near the poles flows towards the equator. However, the motion of the Earth on the equator is very rapid to the east, and as you go towards the poles, this motion slows down, so the motion of the air that flows from the equator also remains rapid to the east, so it reaches the countries towards the poles whose eastward motion is slow. Then it turns to the east. Similarly, the air that flows from the poles towards the equator turns to the west.

The direction of the ocean currents is also the same. The warm current near the Equator from the Gulf of Mexico flows north in the Atlantic Ocean, it then turns to the east and reaches countries like France, England, Norway, etc., on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean in the northeast direction, and the cold current from Greenland flows towards North America. The result of this is that the harbor of Harfangst in Norway, which is at 703 North latitude, remains free of ice for twelve months, whereas the western edge of North America remains covered with ice for more than 40 degrees of latitude due to cold and heat.

Similarly, the warm current flowing north from the Indian Ocean island group turns to the east and keeps the eastern part of Japan warm, and the cold current from the north flows in the exact opposite direction in the China Sea from the western edge of Japan.

This is briefly explained what changes happen in the directions of winds and currents due to the daily motion of the Earth. If you want to know more about this topic, you should use good books of geography.

Except for the motion of this axis, there is another motion in the Earth, by which it completes the orbit of the sun in a year, but it seems as if the sun orbits the Earth. > सकृदुद्गतमब्दार्धं पश्यन्त्यर्क सुरासुराः ।

> पितरः शशिगाः पक्षं स्वदिनं च नराभुवि ॥७४॥

Translation—Sur and Asura keep watching the sun that rises once and see it for half a year continuously, the inhabitants of the lunar world, the ancestors, watch it for one side, and the inhabitants of the Earth, humans, watch it for one day.

Scientific Commentary—The meaning of the first half of this verse is the same as stated in the 67th verse. There is some special meaning in the meaning of the first word of the latter part which needs to be explained. The Sanatana Dharma Hindus believe that the ancestors reside in the upper part of the lunar sphere. This part is not in front of the Earth. Western astrologers also say that the moon revolves around the Earth in such a way that its lower part remains in front of the Earth and the upper part always remains behind.


## Source page 793

Thus, the Moon moves on its axis in the same number of days as it takes to orbit the Earth. Its proof is not difficult. By looking carefully at the lunar image, it is known that its black spots always appear in the same position relative to the edge of the image, which shows that the part of the lunar image facing the Earth always remains in the same condition, that is, the period of the Moon's axis rotation is the same as its orbital period. It can be said that the Moon does not have any axis rotation. But this is not correct. This will be made clear by an example. Place a lamp in the middle and look at it. Suppose the lamp is to your north. Now, while looking at the lamp, move around it in the clockwise direction. When you complete a quarter revolution, the lamp will be to your east. After completing half a revolution, the lamp will be to your south, after three-quarter revolution it will be to your west, and after a full revolution, coming back to the place from where the rotation began, the lamp will be to your north again. This proves that in such a revolution, your face always remains towards the lamp and your back always remains behind it. Also, your body also moves once because while rotating, your face is always towards north, east, south, and west.

When the upper part of the moon always remains opposite to the Earth, what is its relation to the sun? On the day of Amavasya, the moon is between the sun and the Earth, so its upper part remains directly in front of the sun. The Pitris reside in the upper part, so on the day of Amavasya, the sun is directly above the ancestors, meaning it is their noon on this day. That is why obituaries and offerings are done for the ancestors during the noon of Amavasya. On the day of Purnima, it is their midnight. After half of the Krishna Paksha passes, the sun appears to rise while seeing the ancestors, and for half of the Shukla Paksha, it appears to see them equally, meaning the ancestors' morning is on the eighth day of the Krishna Paksha and the evening is on the eighth day of the Shukla Paksha.

Translation—When the orbit of a planet is multiplied by the geodiameter and divided by the earth's circumference, the diameter of that planet's orbit is obtained. By subtracting the geodiameter from the remainder and halving it, the height or distance of that planet from the earth is found.

Scientific Commentary—This is a rule for knowing the diameter from the circumference. Similarly, one should also understand the altitude of other planets.

This revolution circle should also be divided into 360 equal parts. The 'V' place is called the vernal equinox or spring equinox, and the 'SH' place is called the autumnal equinox. The 'K' and 'M' places are called the sine of Cancer and the sine of Libra or the points of South and North transit respectively (see p. 230). With regard to these places, the 'DH' base orbit is called the equinoctial circle and the 'DPMDHPUK' base orbit is called the solstitial circle, because the first has both equinoctial points and the second has both solstitial points. Looking at the table will show that where 12 is written indicates the meridian time. In the next column, 1 is written below and 11 is written above. This means that the portion of the sun is as much as 11 o'clock as it is as 1 o'clock. However, the meridian portion does not differ much from these. In January and December, this difference is not more than two and a quarter degrees. In February and October, it becomes up to 2 degrees. In March and September, it becomes approximately 4. In April and August, it becomes more than 6 degrees. Therefore, this time from the sun's hour cannot be taken very accurately from 1 to 1 o'clock in the winter days.

Time from 1 to 2 o'clock or from 10 to 11 o'clock can be taken easily. Additionally, the knowledge of time in other times can be known with subtlety.

Time from the sun's hour is the pure local time. The time known from the star house clock is different from that. To know the time of the star house clock from the local time, two calculations in local time are required. One is called the time equation and the other is called the longitude calculation. The time equation is positive from January 16 to April 14, after which it remains negative until June 14. After June 14, it becomes positive again and remains so until August. From September to December, it is usually negative. When it is positive, it has to be added to the time of the sun's hour, and when it is negative, it has to be subtracted. Doing this calculation makes the pure local time equal to the mean local time.

Longitude calculation—After knowing the mean-local time, if the position is 1 degree before the longitude line by 82° degrees, then 4 minutes, if 2 degrees before, then eight minutes, and if 10 degrees before, then 40 minutes must be subtracted. But if the position is west of the longitude line by 82° degrees, then it has to be added accordingly. Doing this gives the time which is the time of the telegraph or railway clock.

Sunrise and sunset time—The sunrise time is also given in hours and minutes in the table. If the sunrise time is subtracted from 12 hours, the sunset time will come. This is the time when the center of the sun's image is on the horizon

### Knowing the time by measuring the portion of the Sun—

Example 1—On February 17, the portion of the Sun before noon is 50. What is the time? The portion at 10 o'clock is 47।।। And at 6 o'clock is 57।।। Therefore, the portion of the Sun between 6 and 10 o'clock will be 50. It is also apparent that the portion decreases by 10 degrees between 6 and 10 o'clock. Therefore, in this hour, the portion is decreasing at a rate of 10 degrees per hour, which means it decreases by 1 degree in 6 minutes. There are 7।।। degrees from 57।।। to 50. Therefore, the decrease of 7।।। degrees is in 6 X 7।।। minutes or 46।। mi0. Therefore, the true local time is 6 hours 46 minutes. On this day, the time-equation is + 14 minutes. Therefore, upon giving this calculation, the mean local time is 6 hours 46 minutes + 14 minutes = 10 hours 1 minute. If the place is Allahabad, then 2 minutes should be added. In this way, the railway time is 10 hours 3 minutes. If the place is Kashi, then 2 minutes should be subtracted from ten hours 1 minute, because Kashi is 2 minutes earlier. Therefore, at the time when the portion of the Sun is 50 in Kashi on this date, it would be 6 hours 56 minutes.

Example 2—On March 23, the nataṃśa of the Sun after noon in Patna city is 74 degrees. What time does the railway clock show at this time?

For 26 March, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock is 62. And the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock is 75. In 5 days, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock decreases by 1 degree and the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock decreases by a quarter degree. Therefore, in 2 days, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock will decrease by almost half a degree and the nataṃśa at 5 o'clock will decrease by almost a quarter degree. Therefore, for 23th, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock will be 62. And the nataṃśa at 5 o'clock will be 76. The difference between these two is 13 degrees. This increase happens in 1 hour. Therefore, the speed of increase of the nataṃśa is approximately 4 minutes per degree. But the time of the 74 nataṃśa needs to be known.

To know the latitude of a place—know the meridian altitude (12 o'clock) of the desired day from a table. Then look in the same table what is the meridian altitude of March 21st. Know the difference between both. This is the precession of the sun on that day. Now look at the meridian altitude of your place from the meridian reflection. If the precession is north, adding it to this altitude and if it is south, subtracting it will give the latitude of that place.

Example—The meridian altitude of Raebareli on February 17th is 38.. In the table, the meridian altitude of February 17th is 37॥, and that of March 21st is 25; the difference between these two altitudes is 12. Therefore, the precession of the sun on this day is 120 South. Subtracting this precession from 38॥ gives 26॥, which is the latitude of Raebareli. This is 26. in reality. Therefore, there is an error of a quarter degree in this.

This chapter will be concluded by writing down the method for making a simple sundial. For such a sundial, a sheet of brass with a width of about 3 inches, a length of 15 to 20 inches, and a width of ten or twelve inches will suffice. From this sheet, a right-angled triangle should be cut such that the angle formed on the longer side is equal to the latitude of the place where the sundial is to be installed. A similar right-angled triangle will also be formed in the remaining sheet. Suppose there is a square piece of brass sheet, let's call it T. From this, a right-angled triangle is cut such that the angle of T is equal to the latitude of Prayag, 25^° 25'. The remaining piece is T, in which a line parallel to T is drawn, and the angle U of this line will also be equal to 25^° 25'. Now, from this piece, one should see what kind of circular segment can be cut from it. The center of such a circular segment should be determined, and two parallel lines should be drawn near it, whose distance between them is equal to the width of the sheet and which are perpendicular to the side of T. Then, drawing two equal arcs with the tips of each line as the center. The angle at the center of these arcs should not be less than 60 degrees and not more than 105 degrees because the day length in Prayag is not more than 14 hours. The edges of this circular segment should first be divided at intervals of fifteen-fifteen marks, and then these parts should be divided into three or four equal parts (only three parts are shown in the figure). The parts with fifteen-fifteen marks will indicate the hour, and if there are three parts in each hour, then from each one, twenty minutes can be known, and if there are four parts, then fifteen minutes can be known from each. Smaller parts are not shown in the figure, but in reality, three or four equal parts can also be made from every fourth part, from which five minutes can be known. Such sundials have been installed in the government high schools of Ballia and Raebareli. The sundial of Ballia was prepared under the supervision of a student of the ninth class by this author, but the sundial of Raebareli was made by a mechanic.

Scientific Commentary—These verses show the mutual relationship between the signs, solstices, and seasons. The signs are considered fixed, and their beginning is from the beginning point of Ashwini according to Sūrya Siddhānta, according to which the portion of the celestial star is 180. However, the order of the seasons follows according to the equinoxes, which is moving, so the relationship between the signs, ayanas, and seasons is gradually slipping. There was a time when the beginning of Uttarayana occurred at the same time when the sun's motion also began in the north and it moved towards the north for 6 months. Similarly, the beginning of Dakshinayana occurred at the time when the sun's motion was towards the south in the Cancer sign. But now these two events do not happen together; the sun's northward motion begins 23 days before the Capricorn solstice. In five hundred years, this difference will be about one month. Special discussion has been made on this subject in Triprashnādhikāra. It is an established view of Sūrya Siddhānta that the equinox remains at the 27 degrees of Ashwini, there is no more difference, but this is neither proven by modern science nor accepted by Bhaskaracharya etc. The positions of the Nakshatras mentioned in Brahmanic texts, such as Krittika, prove that the view of Sūrya Siddhānta is not correct (Triprashnādhikāra page 240).

Some scholars also have the opinion, which is well supported on the basis of Brahmanic texts, that the commencement of Uttarayana is not considered from that time.

## Source page 828

Science commentary—at the time when Jupiter comes very close to the Sun, because of the sunlight, it cannot be seen, so it is considered set. Then when it moves so far away from the Sun that it becomes visible, it is considered risen. (See Udaya-stadhikar p. 656-57). This event happens approximately when there is conjunction of the Sun and Jupiter, which used to occur at an interval of about 366 days or 13 months. This period is called 'Varhaspati year'. The names of such years are kept according to the constellations on which the Sun and the Moon are both present at the time of Jupiter's rising or setting. It is stated in the 16th verse that the names of the lunar months are based on the names of those constellations on which the Moon remains in the full moon period, therefore it is proven that the Sun is in the 14th constellation of those lunar months' full moon constellations. For example, in the month of Vaishakh, the full moon falls on the Vishakha or Anuradha constellations, so in this month, the Sun will remain in the 14th constellation of Vishakha or Anuradha, which is Krittika or Rohini. If Jupiter rises or sets at this time, then it is certain that it will also remain on these constellations or one or two constellations ahead or behind, and the new moon will also be on these constellations, therefore Jupiter's 'Kartika year' will begin from this time. That is, if Jupiter rises or sets in the month of Vaishakh, then Jupiter's 'Kartika year' will be applicable, if it rises in the month of Jyeshtha, then 'Varhaspati marg shirsh' year will be applicable, etc. To remove the dilemma between the lunar months and the Varhaspati years, this difference is also made that a 'Maha' is added before the names of the Varhaspati years. However, these Kartik etc. years are not promoted nowadays.

Upon careful observation, it will be apparent that this rule of Sūrya Siddhānta is very loose. The difference between the setting time and the rising time of Jupiter is approximately one month, during which the sun moves more than two constellations. It is possible that at the time of setting, the sun is in the constellation Swati, and at the time of rising, it is in Anuradha. In such a situation, which Varahaspati year should be considered, 'Maha Chaitra' or 'Maha Vaishakh'? Perhaps to resolve this dilemma, Acharya Varahamihira has given this rule in the Brihat Samhita that the name of Jupiter's year should be the name of the constellation in which Jupiter is at the time of rising. Varahamihira has discussed the different results of these years.

The year of Jupiter also has another type called Samvatsara (Chapter on Mean Motions verse 55 and its commentary). These Samvatsaras are discussed in the Panchangs. They are also useful in the mantras of Sankalpa (resolve). There is a cycle of these 60 Samvatsaras. Besides these, there is a cycle of 5 Samvatsaras whose names in order are—(1) Samvatsara, (2) Parivatsara, (3) Idavatsara, (4) Anuvatsara, (5) Idvatsara. They are discussed in Vedanga Jyotisha and Vṛhatsaṃhitā where their results are also stated.

(18) The time between one sunrise and the next sunrise of the sun is called Sawan days. The regulation for performing yajnas is made from the Sawan days. (16) The limit, day, month, and year masters of birth and the vows of Sutak and Chandranyana, the calculation of the mean motion of the planets is done from the Sawan days.

Scientific Commentary — this subject has been well considered in the Chapter on Mean Motions. The periods for which certain actions are to be performed in the Sawan days are counted here. The house where a child is born, or the house where someone dies, is considered impure for ten, twelve, or fifteen days. This is the sutak whose duration is determined according to the Sawan days.

### Of the planets given to you, the course is great. The secret of the world is joined with Brahman.।।27।।

(24) Having said this, Suryaansh departed from Surya Purusha Maya and, being well worshipped by him, went to heaven and entered his circle. (25) Then Mayasur, having obtained this divine knowledge directly from the Lord, considered himself free of sin and grateful. (26) Then the sages, knowing that Maya had received this boon from the Sun God, came to him and asked with reverence while surrounding him. (27) On this, he told them about the great character of the planets, which is like the secret and knowledge of Brahman, and which causes great wonder in this world.

Scientific Commentary—From this it is clear that this astrological text named Sūrya Siddhānta was received by the sages through Maya, who obtained this knowledge from the Sun God or the Suryaansh Purusha through penance. Some scholars draw the conclusion that this text was received from the Yavanas astrologers. In this regard, some thoughts will be written in detail in the introduction without further discussion here.

### Thus the Sūrya Siddhānta, Chapter on Scientific Commentary, Chapter on Mean Motions, Chapter on True Positions, Chapter on the Three Problems

In some texts, a short chapter of 21 shlokas named Vijopanayanadhyāya is found, on which commentators have not commented that the need for Vija-samskara might not have been necessary during the time of the text's composition, so this chapter has been added from the back. In my short opinion, it is possible that what has been written so far has been combined from Suryansh Purusha to Mayasura in this form, but after that Mayasura must have lived for many years and found some difference from his experience, according to which he finally added Vijopanayanadhyāya. Or perhaps some other astrologer after Mayasura extended it. An effort will be made to shed light on this in the introduction. At this time, I also dare to add this chapter.

Scientific Commentary—these are found after the 23rd verse and the first 4 verses of the last chapter of the mānādhyāya and are at least 400 years old because Ranganath ji has mentioned it in his gūḍhārtha prakāśikā ṭīkā written in 1525. This proves that the need to perform seed correction in Sūrya Siddhānta also existed, and our old Acharyas were in favor of making the astrology flawless and comprehensive, not like some pundits nowadays, not the fakirs of the line.

No commentator from here has commented on these verses, so I also consider it useless to translate it because these old seeds are no longer useful. Now it is necessary to fix all calculations with new observations.

Thus, the Scientific Commentary of the fourteenth and last chapter named mānādhyāya of Sūrya Siddhānta has ended.
